EVIDENCE ON THE POINT.—“ Now, you wouldn't believe to look at him that that man was a judge, would you ?" "I don't know as I'd pick him out for a judge; but a glance at his nose would be sufficient to convince me that he had something to do with the bar." THE BREED Nov TO KEEP.—" What! A ,hun- dred eggs a week from twenty hens! Why, I don't get a dozen. Good gracious, Brown, what breed do you keep?" "Oh, Minorcas, Leghorns, and other non-sitting breeds. What are yours ? " "Non-sitters, eh? Well, evidently mine are the non-layers !" "When do you think the moon is at its loveliest, George, dear?" she asked. George, dear, stole his arm round her waist and a glance round the neighbourhood, and answered, When it's behind a cloud, love." And they were as happy as if they were born poets. MILDMAY has never been in the habit of punish. ing his children, leaving that duty to his wife • but I the other day one of them became unruly, and he was obliged to say, "Flora, if you don't keep quiet I shall have to whip you." "Poop !" retorted the child, with a toss of her head, "you isn't the mother."

"Now, George, you know it would be almost wicked of us to marry while you are getting only thirty shillings a week. I'll tell you what we'll do. As soon as you've saved £lOO I will marry you," said Matilda. At the end of three months she asked how much he had saved, and he reported £2 17s. 11d. "'Well, George, dear, I think that's near enough," she said. A CLASS of boys were being asked by their teacher the names of the flesh of various animals. "The flesh of the cow?" "Beef." "The flesh of the sheep ?" "Mutton." At last the flesh of the calf was asked. Up went a boy's hand at the bottom of the class. "Well, Thomas," said the teacher, "what do you say?" "Liver," was the reply. MRS. BRISKE : "Johnny, did the doctor call while I was out ? " Little Johnny (stopping his play); "Yes ma. He felt my pulse an' looked at my tongue, and shook his head and said it was a hopeleB4 case, and he left a perscription, and said he'd call again before night." Mrs. Briske : "Gracious me ! It wasn't you I sent him to see; it was the baby." No REPUTATION FOR VERACITY—.—COUnseI for the defence : "You have heard the testimony of Mr. Brown for the prosecution. Now, did you ever hear Mr. Brown's reputation for truth and veracity questioned?" 'Witness: "Not directly • but he has a baby at his house, he owns a dog, and rides a bicycle, and he is an amateur fisherman." Counsel: "That will do, sir." Counsel for the prosecution: "We do not care to cross-examine the witness, your honour."

"THE growth of a few tiny rootlets," observed the teacher of the botany class, "has been known to lift a rock from its place, and the root of a tree growing out under a stone pavement will some- times push it up and break it. Other cases of a like nature have occurred, I doubt not, within your own observation. Is it not so ?" "Yes, miss," said the boy with the freckles, "I've heard my pa say his last year's wheat crop lifted a mortgage off the farm."

GOT THE RONG TICKET. —Au amusing scene took place the other day at one of the principal Scotch railway stations. A gentleman arrived at the booking-office window just as it closed. "By jove," he said, "I mast get to P— to-day !" A bystander approached, and addressed, him— " Pardon me, sir, but I have a ticket for P— which I cannot use. I shall be de- lighted to let you have it for what it cost me." "Vary well, let me have it; much obliged," and the gentleman hurriedly took his seat. Before starting, the collector came to examine the tickets. The collector looked at it, and said—" Now your own, sir, if you please?" "My own? Why, you have it !" "have you any ideaof travelling with this ticket?" "Certainly. Why not ? " "it is a ticket for a dog."

"SUB WASIIED THE BABY."—A woman walked into the ,bar of a Johannesburg hotel, and picking up the bottle of water used by customers for fur- ther diluting their spirituous liquors, carried it to a side seat. Drawing a piece of soap from her pocket, she commenced to wash the baby which she had in her arms. The barmaid remonstrated with the woman, pointing out that the establish- ment was neither a bath-room nor a lavatory, but the mother continued her infant's toilet, adding, "My husband has his whiskey hare, and he never takes any water with it; so I don't see why I should not use what he ought to." And having washed the baby and re-dressed it, the mother walked out of the bar unconcernedly through a num- ber of astonished spectators.

HE HAD ONE DEFECT.—The girl who had just got engaged was telling the others all about "it," or, more properly, "him." "Yes," she said "I'm very much in love, I know, but not in the blind, silly, illogical way that most girls are. I'm not so far gone but what I can see that he has defe lots of them—both in kola and in charcatcst—h' character. I'm able to regard him, thank good- ness ! from a perfectly impartial and dispassionate standpoint." After which the just-engaged girl proceeded to go into detai According to her "impartial, dispassionate s dpoint "he" was, it seemed, handsome and amiable and clever and courageous and charming and--"I saj-.,,, inter- rupted one of the other girls, isn't this rather one-sided? How about those many defects you said you saw so plainly? Pleas? mention some of them." "Well," said the just-engaged girl heroically, after a minute's silence, "one of hie tront teeth is just a trifle crooked.',

"WOMEN'S CHAT." The coming season in the Deeside Highlands,. 4to be very interesting. For one thing, the famous 8] 1.00 11 , 4 , COng.ie.to take place at Balmoral, and 'MOOS t gdf.4%, toyalty, TiOnl the Queen downs %gbh hap ens to be on Deeside in September, will at, the gathering. Thep there is to be a large tenants,' ball at, the Castle: The ball room has not been much used of late Teats; but it is now having electric light arranged, so that it Will be cooler. When the larg3 number or candles necessary were burnt, it became very hot and uncomfortable to the Queen, who dislikes warm rooms. The Duke and Duchess of Fife have.already gone into residence at New Mar Lodge, and here, during the autumn, they will entertain a number of distinguished guests, including several members of the Royal Family. Lord and Lady Cadogan,on leaving Dublin, will proceed at once to Scotland,to pass the shooting season at Aft rain Forest, Inverness-shire, Lord Cadogan having rented this celebrated shooting from Mrs. Chisholm, of Chisholm. The lodge, which is about twenty-eight miles from Beaulv, is surrounded by magnificent scenery. . _ _

There are rumors to the effect that the Czarina will take a course of waters at Harrogate shortly, which, by the way benefited her so greatly some years ago. She will be accompanied by her children,it is said,the Queen having expressed a wish that they should visit her, more especially the tiny Grand Duchess Tatisna, whom she has not yet scen. There is no doubt that the young Empress of all the Russias has not endeared herself t 3 the women ot her household, by requesting them to discontinue smoking , when at Court. The habit is a confirmed one among 1 Russian women, and that the Czarina should take away their beloved cigarette,is regarded by them as—tyranny. ' Take them as a whole, the women of the Russian aris- tocracy can scarcely be termed fascinating. The ma- jority tuffer from at aa:nia, and this is mostly brought on by late hours, dissipation, over-heated rooms, snick- ing, too much champagne and tea, and the excitement of gambling. Before leaving London,' the Duchess of Sutherland attended a council meeting of the Society of Women JOUrEalikt9, And occupied for the first time the presi- der Val cbair,in which Mrs.Craigie (John Oliver Hobbes) the Bon. Mrs. ,Heriniker, and Mrs. Margnall hays sat before her. The Ouellette i . interest n the sticiety dat4s hick some time and she his already entertained its members within the hospitable doors of Steffnd House. _ . .

Nowadays,' nearly all our ycung Duchesses have bobbies Of some sort. The lovely young Duchess of Sutherland is. as we all well know, devoted to philan- thropy and journalism. The Duchess of Portland is largely interested in temperance work, and a true friend of both Irish and Scotch cottage industries, and tho Duchess of Newcastle finds her great delight in horses and does. The kennels at Cumber have become famous since the Duke of Newcastle married, and there is never a dog show in which Ductless does not interest herself. The Duchess of Newcastle is not pretty, but she has a beautiful figure, and is i4markably discreet. She has no children which is a great trouble t 3 her, more especially so as the next Duchess will be Lady Francis Hope, "May Yohe" best known as the exponent of boy's parts in light operas. The last night of the London season was, after all, taken by Lady Saville, who has entertained for the first time in London, this year. Lady Saville is very young looking, tall, and possesses a beautiful figure. Although she has some very fine jewels, Lady Saville very seldom wears any on her arms or neck, and usually wears only email ornaments in her pretty fair hair, which is always perfectly dreEsed. The ball was given as so many have been this year, in a most informal way. The guests were summoned by visiting cards, (with the d2to and hour scribbled on them, and " come and dance," at the tcp) and by telegram ; friends and acquaintances were stopped in the stneets, carriages ind cabs were hailed, that their occufrants might receive a verbal invitation. The result was, that a little more than fifty sia hours later, everybody who was anybody had congregated to- gether under Lady Saville's hospitable roof. And every- thing was beautifully done. The house was a bower of flowers, the Boor perfect, and the supper—all the heart of 0380 or woman, could desire. The manner in which invitations are usually given now-s-days, has caused the old accepted forms and cere- monies to fade into the limbs of dead and forgotten courtesies. The present mode though is more in ac- cordance with our feelings. There is no time for any- thing, and hurried invitations are but part and parcel of the neural rush and scramble we call the season. I re- member when invitation cards were printed " request the honour," and not even S. the pleasure," when due , ceremony was observed, and an invitation sent out a week or ten days beforehancliwas deemed scant courtesy indeed. As in dress, entertaining, and most other things,tbere Is a fashion in beauty, and there is scarcely a More in- , teresting-study than to compare the recognised types of beauty in the various stages ef the world's history. What is considered beautiful in one generation may be Passed over for the Yeti direct opposite the next. There was a time for instanc'e when smooth glossy • hair was considered charming, but-who wants smooth glossy ,hair nowadays? I have often heard the talk of a girl, an acknaWledged beauty of More than half a century back,svhate only drairbask to perfection was ceneidered to lid in her luxuriant locks, which waned from the roots. This beauty used to spend hours in ironing those locks with a fiat iron on the top and brown paper under- neath, to get rid of the waves ! And to-day, they alone would he sufficient to start a reputation for beauty. Speaking of by-gone modes, it is curious that so grace- ful a woman as the Empress Eugenie (who in the early fifties eet the fashion for Europe) should have inaugura- ted the erinoline. It ruled over us for at least a decade, and a hilf,increasing in size till it reached the dirnen- eiene of Your and a half yards. From time to time we hear rumours concerning the return of this—to put it mildly.eupei floosie addition to our toilette. but in all probability the crinoline will -never be revived in this conntl4. We are all ten &pergola to tolerate such a mode for a moment. Fancy roaniog about from place to place, as is our wont, in trains, Omnibusses, and cabs cfeling, boating, or trying to play golf or tennis, in a crinoline, An eminent man of medicine is of opinion that eycl- ing is the finest thing possible for thence people mentally ffiicted. Thle may be so, of course, and so long as the lunatic's exercise is confined to the grounds of his or her asylum, no one would dream of objecting to the idea. But we dent want any more mad cyclists about the streets. The lives and nerves of pedestrians are too much endangered as it is. In cur large towns and cities we need indeed to have all our senses on the alert to dodge the traffic,and hair-brained cyclists if both sexes. Regiments of mentally afflicted folk, on wheels:, would indeed be the proverbial last straw on the camel's back. , Detached coats are being built in either tan, white, or black. div.head: LADIES' LETTER
div.p: LADIES' LETTER

Mr DWI NELLTB. Holiday-making seems quite the fashion mr the hour. It has been noticed. that foulards o 1 the patterned type are much in evidence at our seasids - resorts. These can be made quite simply fdr morning wear, or so elaborated that they form really dressy afternoon toilettes. Satin foulards with a bright satin surface, and rather less pattern than on the ordinary foulard, are quite the latett fashion, but in the bright blues and mauves now I affected are rather conspicuous. Some of tte better class printed sateens and cottons closely re- semble foulard, and are delightful for morning wear, more especially in light gray-blues, in pd..e heliotrope, or in navy or Royal blue, with neat rings or spots. Materials of this kind, made with one of the new flounced skirts, lightly trimincil with narrow insertion lace, and a pretty blouse, are most useful for seaside or country wear.

As to millinery you do not require to be informed that Dame Fashion is full of vagaries and that the modes are ever changing. This season the hats worn are of the large type and they are mostly laden with feathers. Some, however, have a plenitude of ribbons and flowers, and for the most part they are extremely becoming.

A gown which I recently saw and admired was a charming combination of grass lawn, fine yellow lace, and thin black lace insertion, with a band and knot of velvet, the hat bearing a wealth of ostrich feathers. This gown was mounted on a fine silky sateen, or glace silk or mery could be used.

Capes have by no means lost favour, bat the style is changing considerably, and at present this species of wrap is less protective than a yore, and it will need extensive revision or much addition before it is feasible for wititer wear. Just now it is a charming wrap for the late summer and early autumn, and the rounded fronts leave the arms free, and give a glimpse of a pretty bodice or belt.

Where the banded bodice is worn, belts are now made in corselet fashion, but only about one-third of the depth formerly worn, and being cut on the cross, these lie very fiat, and the edge rests on the skirt, thus relieving the unsightly gap so often perceptible between the belt and the top of the skirt. These belts are unlined, and the centre back is drawn down to a slight point, where it is secured by a concealed satey-pin. These belts are very attractive in colour on black chiffon blouses, which can be worn with black skirts, and are very smart for general wear. For instance, a belt and folded stock of turquoise-blue have a charming effect on black chiffin, and are light and cool with black skirts. Hats are now so smart that these touchee in the costume make a very attractive tout ensemble. Black costumes, slightly relieved with steel sequins, are extremely f ishionable this season, and the skirt is usually of satin or peau de sole, trimmed with chiffon, and worn with a blouse in black chiffon, on which steel sequins are disposed in some attractive fashion. Handsome blouses of chiffon, elaborately twiked and gauged, coat very little more than the entire cost of material and making, allowing, of course, for a good dressmaker, and so expertly are these blouses made, that the fragile chiffon looks scarcely touched, even with its innumerable tucks and frills. Very pretty mantles for young ladies' wear are of plisse chiffon, cut along in rows, and the edge partiatly ironed out, which leaves pretty little frills, which are supplemented by a frill 'of lace, and extra frills are placed at the edge. Pink, pale blue, white, and yellow are used in this style, and the lining is of the same shade as the crimped chiffon. Very dressy mantles of matronly fashion are of gauze de chambrey, mounted on orange silk, which colour is wearable with almost any gown. An effective shape has a dolman-back, ending ins deep point, the sides in cape form rounding off in front.
Your loving JENNIL

A WARMOF THE KING. • - -7- By KATHARINE S. MACQI7OrD, Author of "Maisie-Derrick," "The story of Lois," "Patty," "Louisa," -"At the Red Glove," "Miss Eyon of Eyoncourt," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Jeanne Kerg-rist, a wealthy heiress and an only child, has become on her father's death ward of - the King.of France. Jeanne is only thirteen when the King commands her to tinny the Count of Laval, who is twenty years her senior. The story opens in the garden of Jeanne's house, where Jeanne tells her friend and playfellow, Rolland, of her dislike to the proposed marriage. Rolland, a fine young fellow, dislikes it too. He has been brought up with Jeanne, and, if he were richer, would marry her when she grows up*. The Count of Laval comes to the castle, accompanied by a handsome young cousin, Gilles de Rota. Jeanne likes the Count, but she takes a dislike te De Beta, who flatters and pities her. He and the Count of Laval leave the castle directly after the marriage ceremony.. Four years later. Jeanne's mother dies. Rolland has been away fighting in Italy,and the Netherlands. Jeanne is i alone n the world, and her husband falls ill. He sends De Betz to fetch his young wife home to Laval.. Jeanne is seventeen, an has become beautiful. She travels in a litter to Laval, accom- panied-by her maids and her mother's woman Gillonne, ,a courageous and clever Bretonne. They reach Laval at the end of four days and learn that Jeanne's husband, the Count, is dead. De Beta is now Count of Laval, and Gillonne suspects his intentions towards her mistress. She resolves to seek help and advice from her widowed mistress's friend Rolland, who has now become a Viscount. Jeanne asks the Count of Laval to take her to Amboise to seek protection from her guardian, the King. Laval consents. He is determined to marry Jeanne, whose wealth, position and beauty attract him. He is also bent on capturing the Constable of Bourbon, lately declared guilty of high treason. Jeanne and her escort leave Laval. Gillonne quits her mistress on the pretext of seeking a relative, and narrowly escapes being murdered by two of Laval's soldiers, who accompa'ny her. Laval tells Jeanne that the King has left Aroboise, and they journey in search of him.

- CHAPTER IX. TO BOWAN& Jeanne had fared better than her woman had done, but she already regretted her consent to Gillonne's journey. Anne and Matlrnrine were excited by this change from the usual monotony of their lives, and their mistress saw with'vexation that when the young. Count engaged her in talk her two maids cast aside the reticence taught by their prudent duenna, and talked and laughed with any of the soldiers who made free to speak to them. • Jeanne was disturbed, she knew that her mother had never. permitted this kind of licence when they had now and then journeyed to Lannion, or to Guingamp. The young Countess loved riding-, the day, bright, with a touch of freshness inAhe air, was exhilarating, and as she looked around her the dark cloud of sorrow that had settled on her spirits lifted ;' she put her horse to a canter, 'feeling that she could do 'nothing in the way of surveillance, and that therefore there was no use in meeting possible evil half-way. Laval—she could hardly think of him by the new name—kept close beside her, and she was obliged to own that he made a gallant, knightly figure on the powerful horse, which he .managed with the ease of an experienced rider ; he wore steel back and breast-plate over ,his doublet; a very long sword hung besidehis thigh, and in his richly- ornamented belt were a dagger • and a brace of piaols; his black Velvet cap, fringed by a white e h feather and looped up with rich jewels, was now exchanged for a stel sad-piece, vefy becoming to his dark face and handsome eyes; Jeanne was obliged to own to herself they were. jiandsome, though she still thought their expression was sinister. On the second day Laval said: "I have =news, madame; 'which will, I fear, disappoint you." She looked at him, her eyes full of question. "The King is, I believe, on his way., to Lyons; I hear that his Majesty tra'velled a few days ago to Moulins, in order to visit the Conetable de Bour- bon, who is indisposed. Finding the Constable still too ill to join him, the King has probably proceeded on his wpy to Lyons, where, as, you may have heard, madame, troops from all parts of France are assembling." Jeanne'e bright face clouded over. "Does the Court follow the King to Lyons, monsieur ? " "Not at present, madame; it is said that his Majesty intends to take command of the army, which it is supposed is almost ready to march for Italy." • = • " Jeanne smiled again; she saw a hope of release from her unpleasant position. "I thank you, monsieur, for your kind intention of escorting melo'the Royal presence, but I prefer to go to Amboise ; I shall be safe there in the care of my cousin, the Countess of Chateaubriand." De Retz looked at her with an unpleasant smile. "How unfortunate!" he exclaimed. "I had understood, madame, that you wished to be placed as soon as possible under, the protection of his Majh esty; therefore, when I learnt that the King was on is•way which lies some leagues above Amboise. We shall to Lyons, I took the road to Blois, reach Blois this evening, and if we travel part of the night we may soon come up with the King's rearguard; I shall then be able to learn the precise line of route followed by his Majesty." Jeanne threw back her hood, and looked fixedly

_ at him. "I am sorry to derange your plans, monsieur, but I must ask you to escort me to A.mboise." In spite of the mask she wore, he could see she looked determined. He smiled at her courage. "Dear lady," he said with deference, "I dare not take on me to set aside express commands. The orders of my dear lord and godfather were precise; in the event of your becoming a widow, I was to take you to the presence of your guardian, King Francis ; there was no mention of Amboise or of any other Royal palace. I promised to render up my charge to his Majesty in person. It will, however, gratify me to escort you later on wheresoever the Bing may please to send you, whether it be to Longnedee or to Amboise ; I dare not, however, take you any- where till I have received his Majesty's Royal i nstructions. "

He saw that she was angry; he noted that the ear nearest him had become red as a damask rose. "I do not understand, monsieur. How was it •that before we quitted Laval you bade me, if I pleased, remain there for the present? How could you venture to say this if your orders were so peremptory? Ido not understand!" She spoke angrily and with some disdain. Laval was secretly amused, but he sighed, as if her words pained him. "You judge me harshly, madame; that is, how- ever, natural. Will you piermit me to explain myself? I had the, idea of leaving you at Laval, in order that I might hasten to Amboise to inform the King of the sad event by which you had become a widow, and to ask his Majesty's intentions regarding you. I then found that you did not wish to remain at Laval, and I agreed that we should travel together to Amhoise. Only yesterday I had tidings that the King was at Moulins; I learn to- day that he has left ,the town, and is on his way to Lyons. I trust, madame, that this explanation satisfies yon ? " He looked So much in earnest, the explanation sounded so plain and probable, that Jeanne felt ashamed of her doubts. There was,: however, somethinm repugnant to her in being taken to the camp, NOiere probably there would only be men with the King. She thought for some minutes before she answered: "I will go with you, monsieur, on one condition: you must leave me in some village with a small escort while you go forward and learn his Majebty's intentions regarding me." .11e Mso hesitated to answer ; but it seemed to him. as he considered Jeanne's proposal, that it fitted marvellously with his designs. The,story he had just been telling the girl was time, but the arrangement of facts was .garbled. He knew before he quitted Laval that the King was 013 his way to visit the Constable at his palace at Moulins—in other words, to arrest his powerful subject since then he had learnt that the King had hiniself convinced .of his Royal o:l3in 'F g4od faith, and that at parting from llim llourbon had promised. to follow the King to Lyons ai soon 'is he recoiered from the illness which had kept him in bed during his Sovereign's Visit.

Laval waq determined to marry the young widow, besides his desire .to possess the handsome dowry bequeathed to her, and her own rich inheritance, her beauty strongly attracted him ; but he knew that he could not -marry' , her. without the King's leave, and last night new had reached him from Moulins ihich seemed to orvi a direct way to his purpose,

CHAPTER X. FOR THE CONSTABLE.

Gildee lived till they reached Blois, in answer to her inquiries Jeanne learnt that during the night the faithful fellow had passed away. She grieved for his loss; she felt that he had been the only man in whom she had felt trust among the rough and, for the most part, evil-looking soldiers. Jeanne noticed that Laval became more and more attentive to her; he now always rode beside her, and he evidently tried to beguile the wearisomeness of the journey by sprightly talk. The road became more and more monotonous. Laval avoided the larger towns, he even made a circuit to avoid Bonrges, of which city Jeanne had heard much, and would have liked a nearer view, so greatly was she fascinated by the appearance in the distance of its cathedral on the hillside; but Laval told her they might not delay; every large city, he said, meant, with soldiers, a delay of at least some hours. They reached Moulins in the evening light, and after so many long days in the saddle Jeanne and her women looked pale and exhausted. Laval was unwilling to lose time, but he had to make some icquiries in the town, and he resolved to halt longer than usual. He therefore divided his party, leaving the greater number of his soldiers in Moulins, while, with only a couple of men, the Countess and her two women, he sought out a quiet inn on the south side of the town. - lie stopped before a large rambling building which seemed to have seen better days, for the beams which supported its projecting upper storey were richly carved, as were also the bargeboards of the gables above them. It was evidently a hostelry, for a sign- board projected from its front, bearing the emblem of a heart, with the legend of "Le Coeur Loyal." Jeanne thought the house looked homely enough, and as they crossed the spacious kitchen to gain the stairs leading to the bedchambers she noted that the place looked cleaner than most of the hostels in which they/ had lodged during the journey. She also saw that the widowed hostess, a woman of middle age, had a singularly frank face. The bed- chamber to which she was shewn was gloomy, a long low, room with heavy beams in the ceiling; it was lit by one lattice window with heavily leaded panes; a vine trained over it had freed itself from bondage, and rapped now and then an ominous warning against the glass as gusts of wind blew its sprays to and fro. The hostess had shewn the way upstairs, and without waiting for orders she opened the door of $ closet beside the chimney, took out a flint and stesl and kinhtinc wood. and proceeded to set fire

The relative holding effect of nails is considered in a paper read recently be Professor Soule before the Technical Societo of the Pacific Coast. Experiments described in the paper show that, under all Ordinary conditions, cut nails held better than wire nails. Holding effect increases wills the length of a nail but not in proportions expressible by any simple formula. When it Is properly pointed, the held of a cut nail is increased by 33 per cent. Nails driven into some woods. Californian redwood, for example, will take a better hold the longer they are left In ; the reverse happens with other woods, Dongtas pine, for Iry tance. Deals, when nailed to a block, show about equal bolding powers for equal areas of nail, whether a few thick nails or a great-r number of thin Bails are employed ; the advantage is slightly in favour of the- thick nails. div.p: (CoPYrigitio)
CYCLING AND CYCLISTS.
No. VII.—LONG - DISTANCE ROAD- RIDING AND RACING.
BY T. A. EDGE (EDITOR OF THE "CYCLERS' NEWS").

The great secret in long-distance riding is the possession of stamina. The best long-distance riders are born, and not made, for their very nature has the inherent qualities necessary to the game. Stamina can, however, be cultivated to a very large extent by many, and, whether natural or not, train- ing to develop the withstanding of fatigue is abso- lutely essential to all. lam writing these hints rather in the interests of amateur riders than of professionals, for it can be taken for granted that the last-named class have a perfect knowledge of their art—if one can call cycle-riding such—whilst they have their trainer's watchful eye to look over them. The professional has all his time at his dis- posal, the amateur has to snatch his training hours from his spare time in the evenings or on Saturday afternoons and Sunday—there are few men who do not ride on the Sabbath nowadays. Let us say the cyclist has his bicycle and intends to ride on the road—path work I will deal with afterwards. If he has not done any preliminary work, it is necessary to start steadily, the idea being to build up the System slowly; be careful the mistake so common is not made, that of being too anxious to get into form quickly, which is an impossibility. Hard work 'Without injury can only be indulged in when the body has been gradually worked into a condition to Withstand it. For the first fortnight, then, slow rides in the evening, with a longer ride on Sunday; never let the pace exceed eleven or twelve miles an hour. By this means you will get your muscles Into a hard and fit state, ready for the SEVERER TRIALS TO FOLLOW.

In about three weeks the athlete will be able to Spurt a little up the hills, and will find that he can ride much easier and without fatigue. He can now indulge in hard, fast riding, for the cultivation of speed, for it does not matter how much you may be able to stay, even for very long distances; you must have speed, for never was there a wiser say- ing than that it is "the pace that kills." Path work is absolutely essential to road-riding, and after the first few weeks, with the exception of long rides on Saturday and Sunday, an hour's ride or more on alternate evenings on the path, behind pacemakers When possible, will improve both speed and staying I"fers. Seine men require more work than others, ac- "ding to their build. A spare man naturally citesnot need the hard exercise the man who is of 'meshy build will. Of the cyclists I know who made .1,.1„.e5h quickly, M. A. Holbein stands out by himself. 'me had to reduce his weight by several stone before he was able to ride at all well. Prank Shorland, on the other hand, was of the thin, spare class, and when he first started had—in or out cf training—not an ounce of superfluous flesh about llolbein required a lot of hard work. At times he would walk some thirty miles a day for days together in order to reduce himself and give him the requisite stamina. This brings to mind that walking is the finest exercise that can be possibly taken to bring oneself into condition. The exertion is not great, but the stain ma derived there- from cannot be over-estimated. When the roads are sloppy or slippery, walking will ,be found an ex- cellent substitute for cycling, and equally beneficial. Some two or three years back I met G. P. Mills at One of the cycle shows. "Are you game to try and teak the twenty-four hours and

div.head: LAND'S END TO JOAN 0' 'GROATS
div.p: LAND'S END TO JOAN 0' 'GROATS

r"°rds with me on a tandem?" he asked. "Cer- tini.. , a„ , y I replied. "Then get fit," was his answer. I commenced to train about Easter, but, unfor- tunately, fell and put my shoulder out. Of course, I could not ride a bicycle under the circumstances, and the whole of my training for the twenty-four hours was done by walking, with but a few long rides on the front seat of a Humber tandem tricycle, and a bicycle to finish up with. Yet I never remember having ridden better. Walking is, how- ever, monotonous work at the best. After five or six weeks' practice you will be in good condition, and can go long Tides with im- punity. If you are training for a twenty-four hours' ride, it is necessary that you should now put in some long, hard spins. Ride on Sunday about one hundred rid thirty to one hundred and fifty miles. The gradual work you have done will enable you to do this at a good pace, and your evenings can be devoted to the path. Two or three nights during the week at the most on the path and these long • rides on the road on Sundays will, in a short time, bring you into the pink of condition, and you will be ready to enter your contest, whether against the watch or an opponent—but trials against , the watch are the more popular now. My advice has been given for long distances, but if racing for fifty or a hundred miles practice behind pacers on the path is necessary. For fifty miles races I believe in about fifteen miles fast work with vary- mg rides over almost the full distance, but not quite at full pace. . ever, if possible, over•exert yourself in train- log. There has been many a race left on f trainino• oTouud. If a man is preparing for ,Paced race's he will require constant practice uehind pacemakers. The art of "hanging on" to PerEeCtiOTl is only acquired by practice. Presuming Your training has finished, say after three months— for the longer and more easy the preparation the better form is likely to result—you will now think of the actual contest. In long-distance rides—l am sPeaking of twenty-four hours', whether against the watch or competitors—much depends upon your arrangements. Yout;
PACEMAKERS MUST ,BE CHOSEN

with heads as well as legs. Many a record and many a race have been thrown away through the pacers not knowing their business, being too anxious, and racing the man they are taking care of Oft his legs. Judgment in pace is a quality that a good long-distance rider must have. It is so easy when one fads well to ride too fast and bring On what is known as a bad time. The man with judgment will so regulate his pace that the bad time Will not come, and by continual riding at an average aPeed will, without bursts and the accompanying a of slows, accomplish a much better performance. The pacers must be-men with a thorough knowledge of a bicycle, be able to repair a tyro or a machine quickly, whilst they should have suitable food ready for the rider, and know exactly wha I to do in cases of emergency. All the best road rides have been dorm by men who have made the best arrangements, having had pacers to take them the various stages and see that no time was lost at the stopping,-place3. Make your time-sheet out, and as nearly as possible—taking into consideration changes in wind and state of roads—to keep to it. In record-breaking, study well what you have ; to do before you make an attempt, and, once started, whilst you have any possible hope never be 12'ersuaded to give up. It is absolute nonsense to attempt long-distance races or records if you do not reake up your mind to go through to the end with them, no matter how bad you feel. Have your unrid centred on the goal in view, and do not listen to anyone who tries to dissuade you from it. When racing, a man should never give in; if you feel I bad, stick to your guns, or rather, bicycle; you can depend upon it that your opponent is not feeling very Well; ell ; and time and time again I have seen a Plucky arid determined rider make a less determined °Eke give way by sheer gameness, or snatch a record the merest margin when noes RAD ALL BUT GONE. (X 0 over your arrangements for pacing and feeding very carefully before starting, and see that your bicycle or bicycles are right. Then place yourself its the hands of one man to engineer your ride, and don't worry yourself. But be careful in yout choice of the man who shall look after you. He in.ust have judgment, presence of mind to do the r_ight thing under difficulties, smartness in takini :vantage of everything in your favour that presents we'4lr• and untiring energy on your behalf. Food
I

for long-distance riding in actual contests con. sits of slops—stewed and ripe fruit, porridge and milk, eggs beaten up in tea, soda and milk or lemonade, beef-tea, chicken-broth, &c. Some riders prefer one thing, others another. I have not previously spoken about gears, for what gear will suit one man will not be found quite right for another; they are simply a matter of choice, but always remember to err on the low rather than on the high side. Clothing.—On the road the C.T.C. coloured flannel suits, unlined, with sweater or flannel shirt, stockings, &c., will be found the best. Unlined clothes can be dried quickly,and extra warmth can be obtained by using an extra sweater. In training for path long-distance races, road work is not necessary for races up to twelve hours; it will rather be found hurtful, for it will decrease the speed qualities of the rider. Riding a couple or three hours at a stretch behind pacers, on the track when possible, will give you actual experience. If you are compelled to de most of your work unaided, then the fastest possible work behind pacers, occasionally, even for a few miles, will be found greatly bene- ficial. In twenty-four hours' rides on the path, in addition to path work, long slow rides on Sunday on the road will bring you the necessary ability to sit in the saddle for a long time; but I should not advise hard plugging on the road; it will take away from your speed, and that is absolutely needful in path racing, no matter what the distance may be. In actual racing your arrangements must be very complete, and the man whom you place reliance on must be able to feed you properly, as you cannot get off your machine in path racing often. The

div.head: PACING IN A3LAPAIJR CONTESTS
div.p: PACING IN A3LAPAIJR CONTESTS

is very peculiar, and you need to use more judgment in amateur than in professional races to get the best of this. I need not dwell upon the advantages of sticking a man in a race, but you must be to particularly careful about some men, who never get on the machine with the idea of riding the contest out, and who go fast in fitful spurts. These men are dangerous in a degree. Refrain from sprinting in a twenty - four hours' race, or in any long distance race whenever it can be avoided. Go steadily at one uniform pace. Sprints take more out of a man than anyone can imagine, and the rider who goes along steadily will be riding at the same pace when the gallery riders have left the track or are crawling along at a gait which is disgusting. Remember that in long-distance racing everything depends upon the way in which you are paced, careful judgment in riding and feed- ing, as a twenty-four hours race is not won in the first twelve hours, and a man who can ride a good second twelve hours is sure to beat more men than will beat him. I have not dealt with the question of riding longer distances than twenty-four hours, because I hardly think it necessary; so few care about it. _ _

Many men are doubtless anxious to know if long-distance riding has any injurious effect. My personal experience, which commenced twenty years ago on the tall bicycle, leads me to say no. I have ridden four 1,000 miles records on the road, two Land's End to John o'Groat's records, twenty-four hours, and other races and record rides too nume- rous to mention, and the result of my training and riding has been to leave me thoroughly strong and •healthy.

div.head: ST. JOHN AMBULANCE BRIGADE, WARRINGTON CORPS.
div.p: ST. JOHN AMBULANCE BRIGADE, WARRINGTON CORPS.
VISIT TO THELWALL.

. - - Last Thursday afterncon the members of the above brigade, accompanied by their wives and lady friends to the number of about 160, drove from the Central Station to Cuerden Hall, Thelwall, on the invitation of Mr. R. A. Naylor and Miss Naylor. On arrival the party formed up in procession, headed by the flag and the ambulance trophies in possession of the Corps in the following order, viz :—The Warrington and District Diamond Jubilee Challenge Shield, and the Cheshire Lines Ist and 3rd prize challenge cups, which were borne by Superintendent Buckley, let officer Williams and 3rd officer E lwards respectively, representing the winning teams. A cordial welcome was extended to the party by Mr. and Miss Naylor, and the house and grounds were thrown open for their inspectien. Mr. Birtles, of War- rington, then photographed those present, positions being taken up on the sters and balcony of the Hall by the hon. surgeons, officers, and members, the ladies,and Mr- and Miss Naylor. Afterwards a demonstration of ambulance work was given by a bearer section of 16 men, including stretcher and hand seat drill, bandaging and cases of supposed suffocation, under the command of Superintendent Buckley and Ist officer Williams. Various games and other amusements were pro/aided and the party thoroughly enjoyed themselves. A good substan- tial tea was provided by Mr. Naylor in the schoolroom. After which an impromptu concert was given. Songs, recitations, etc, were given by Mr. and Miss Naylor, Mr. Kildeff,Mr. and Mrs.Greaves,two Mrs.Edwards,and Mr. Fred Taylor. The officers present included Captain War- ing,chief auperintendent;hon.surgeene,Dra.Bower and J. Guest Gornall;lst Officer Williams,2nd Officer Mansseur, and Srd Officer W. Edwards. Speeches were given by Mr. Naylor on the usefulness of tha Ambulance Cause, and Captain Waring, on the work,and devotion given to the cause by Mr. Hardy, who expects to be removed from this district Shortly. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. and Miss Naylor for their kindness and generosity on the motion of Captain Waring, and after singing the National Anthem the party drove home, thoroughly pleased with their second visit to Tbelwall.

PASSING .BASE COIN AT NEWTON RA.CES. At the Warrington Occasional Court,last Friday.bef ore Mr. J. Frost, Mary Browne, 4, East-street, Thomas-et., Belford, Manchester, was brought ,up on a charge of Passing base coin at Newton Races, on the 12th and 13:h July.—Richard Johnson licensee of the Birmingham Arms Hotel, Chester, said he had a refreshment booth on the Newton race course on the 12th and ff.3th July. On the 13th July one of his waitressm brought him a 23. piece about 11 o'clock in the morning. After converse- tionbe followed her to the bar and she pointed out the prisoner to him. Be then recognised her as the person who had passed a bad half-crown on another waitress., lie told prisoner that the 2s. piece was a bad one and asked her if she had any more bad coins on ber. In a couple of hours after, during which she had not left the bar, the prisoner ordered two bottles of beer. One of the waitresses (Maggie Moasy) picked up the 23, piece she put dawn and brought it to him. He went to the prisoner and said "This is bad. Have you plenty of these bad coins on your She replied "L do not know wherever I kave got thern.Someone must have paid them to tee." He gave her in charge to P.C. Leerning.—Mrs. Taylor (wai'ress at the booth) also gave evidence.--P.O Leming said he charged prisoner with passing two had florins, and one counterfeit half-erown She had a blac k satchel with her fa which were thirty .bsd half-crown and four bad 2s. pieces. She eaid in answer to the cl arge that she found the bag.—Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

A delightful addition to the public "lungs " of London has been secured by the acquisttion of a lovely estate adjoining Hampstead Heath. The pur- ohn,e, moreover, reAcues one of the most charming pots in the immediate neighbourhood of the metro- polis from the hands of the speculative builder. A committee had been formed to rescue the hill for the public, but tlot<yr only saw their way to offering £35,000, and the estate, therefore was put up to auc- tion. The offers of the building competitors carried the price beyond that figure,but a private capitalist was resolved that the splendid panorama should not be destroyed by streets and villas, and went on capping every builders' offers until the estate was knocked down to him. He then offered it to the committee at cost price, and, the County Council and several of the vestries coming to the rescue, almost the total amount has been made up.

Since Mr. Balfour's surrender on the Vaccination Bill the anti-vaccinationists are expecting great things from the magistrates. It is believed that the local bench will never run counter to local feel- ing, and they count upon the p.issibility of its be- ing well manned with magistrates who are even in sympathy with them. This is true enough as re- gards certain localties where feeling runs high,but the same thing does not quite follow in towns or country districts,whera the anti-vaccinationists are not strong in numbers. But the most strenuous advocate of vaccination, or even the most strenuous county bench, has not any loophole left for ' giving trouble if an objector acts in the spirit of Mr. Balfour's speech explaining his own clause, for the bench has no right to enter into the grounds of the opinion formed by the conscientious objector. These may be perfectly foolish and inconclusive. He has simply to stand stolidly and firmly by the posi- tion that he believes vaccination will be injurious to the health of his child,and the bench has no alter- native but to give effect to his objection.

It is reported in scientific quarters that, owing to want of funds, the Ben Nevis Observatories will cease to exist in Octobcr next. By the establish- ment of these observatories and the unique hourly observations made at them by night and by day without a break over a period of fifteen years, a great experiment has been carried out with signal success, though at considerable cost. A sum of no less than £18,150 has, I learn, been expended on the scheme, and this has been obtained by contribu- tions, partly from scientific bodies, but mainly from the public. It is felt that the time has arrived when these first-class meteorologicA observatories should be continued by the State, and it certainly does seem a matter for deep regret that these two stations, both well equipped and in full working order, should have to be closed. It is satisfactory to know that in a large measure the objects aimed at have been attained. Nothing similar to the observations made outside in the severe climate of the top of Ben Nevis has at yet been done at any other high-level observatory in the world. They furnish an invaluable mass of material for the study of meteorological phenomena.

There is a great deal of apprehension among the members who have favoured the modifications made by the Government in the Vaccination Bill that the House of Lords may reverse certain of the amendments voted at the instance of the anti- vaccinationists. It is understood that if this is done the Government will he asked to drop the bill, and as they appear to be bent on bringing the session to a close by Saturday, the measure is in some danger. It has, however, this chance, that a large number of the peers will be out of town before it reaches the House of Lords. It is expected that there will be a three or four hours' discussion on the third reading in the House of Commons on Monday.

It is confidently stated that the report of the ex- perts appointed by the Rome Office to investigate the extent of the evils of lean-poisoning in the Potteries and to suggest remedies practically con- firms the worst which has been said in recent de- bates about the seriousness of the evils, and sug- gests drastic remedies. This report is now in the hands of the Home Secretary, and it is feared that it may be treated as a confidential document. Mem- bers who have taken up the cause of the pottery workers naturally desire the publication of the re- port, and every effort will be ,made to compel the Home Office to make it public without delay.

A visit to 49, Pall Mall, where the thousand and one articles necessary for a sojourn in the Arctic zone have been gathered together, will materially help to a better understanding of the rigours which the members of the Newnes-Borchgrevink expedi- tion will have to encounter in the South Polar re- gions. All kinds of furry armour are there to render 1 them proof against extremes of temperature, and modern skill has brought these articles of rough reindeer skin almost to the point of luxury. An outfit of camel-hair fleece. complete with blizzard- proof helmet,is sufficiently soft and downy to please the most fastidious taste. The stock of boots and of snow-shoes also is extensive and well adapted to varying circumstances. The tents of draught-proof green Willesden canvas, the sleeping bags, the aluminium cooking service, and many other neces- saries seem well calculated to promote comfort under difficult conditions, while the store of com- pressed flesh and vegetable foods includes much that is not only nutritious but also tempting. In such an expedition dogs,of course, are an important consideration. The pack of seventy Samoyuds were not on view at Pall Mall to-day,but there were some excellent facsimiles of the animals, which are the firs; of their kind ever brought to this country. They will be under the charge of a couple of Finns, whose picturesque summer tent was a conspicious 'item in the exhibition. The coverings, shoes. and I harness of the dogs have been the object of much attention, and 28 tons of biscuit have been laid in for their consumption. The Southern Cross, which is to convey the explorers to the Antartic,is shortly due from Norway. Next to the celebrated From, she is said to be the strongest vessel of her kind.

The correspondence published on Tuesday be- tween the Fire Brigade Department of the County Council and Messrs. Yarrow and Ca., the ship- builders at Poplar, shows that the department has put itself into an entirely false position. In Bis- mark's language, it has put its foot a great deal further out than it will be able to keep it, and there is nothing before it but an ignominious retreat. It was prepared to give the firm a contract for a &a- float costing 48,000, but it stipulated, among manY other things, for the rig'ot of dismissing the firm:s foreman if it saw fit, Of course, a proposal of this kind was rejected by the firm, and the department, if it goes up and down the shipbuilding yards of Britain, will only meet with the same reply, The Council has done much to raise the conditions of labour in the metropolis, for which working rarp are unquestionably grateful, but Bismarg s Aphorism is a sound one.

It seems to be tolerably well settled in the mind of most army men that the Duke of Connaught will vatate his command at Aldershot in October. This bears out the rumours to which I have more than once referred, that there will be a vacancy in the ()ince of commander-in-Chief about the same time. Sir Bedvers Buller will naturally succeed the Duke, and the Duke will naturally step into the place vacated by Lord Virolseley. The Canadian Governor- Generalship has not been reserved for Lord Weise- ley, as was expected in many quarters, and what he is destinded for is at present given up as an in- soluble problem. As several years of his command have still to run, he cannot have been cleared out to make way for the Duke's advancement, without adequate compensation of an official kind being in prospect for him;but even in military clubs specula- tion iz silent as to what it can possibly be _

A NOCTURNE AT SMOLENSK.

His adventures for that night did not end with his escape from the den of thieves. As, with a frost-bitten foot, he made his way painfully through the snow, stumbling now over a deserted gun-carriage, now over a c xpse, once stopping just in time to avoid a fall from the top of the ramparts into the Dnieper, which flowed in a turbid, icy stream at their foot, he became, or fancied he became, aware of music like the notes of an organ floating in the air. Just then a heavier fall than usual, over the body of a dead dragoon, caused him to utter a cry ot pain. It was answered bye shout at no great distance; and, making his way tower& the sound, Bourgogne found to his joy that it proceeded from a friend of his—one Beloque, a sergeant in the same corps keeping guard ever two sick men. who, unable to go further, were awaiting the b3arers for whom he had sent. To him he recounted the adventure of the cellar. "But," he adds, " I did not dare to say anything about the music, lest he should say I was ill." The pair walked up and down, their conversation broken at times by the death-rattle from one or another of the sick men, when suddenly the serial music began to sound again, this time appearing to to much nearer at hand. Beloque said, in a whisper, lest the dying men should ovethear— a curious touch of the courtesy which a Frenchman, if he has time to think, seldom fergets—"lt is very like the music of the dead. All is dead around us, and I , have a pretentimeut that in a few days! shall bi dead too. Well I God's will be done. But one might die with less suffering. Look at those poor fellows." 'I made no answer," sass the narrator, "but my thought was the same as his." For a while they listened in silence, disturbed only by the laboured breathing of one of the sick men. The sounds seemed to proceed from overhead. Presently they ceased, and with a plaintive cry the other mac drew his last breath. The b iarers came up, and the survivor was taken away. Bourgogne and his friend went with the party ; but the former soon left them, and went in goat of another comrade. At once the mysterious music began again, and, following it, he arrived at a building a'l lighted up. This proved to be a church. Climbing over the low churchyard walhand crossing some ground, which seemed straneely uneven till he perceived that it was strewn with corpses lying under a covering of snow, the sergeant reached the doorway. The door was open, and volumes of smoke , issued from it. The interior wee also thick with smoke, amid which men were singing and playing the organ ; but this presently cleared as the flame of the fire burnt up ; and one of the singers recognised Bourgogne, and greeted him. They turned out to be men of his own company, ail more or less drunk. Boole of them, being on fatigue duty, had seen two Jews emerging from a cellar. Marking the spot, they had returned, found some brandy and some food as well as some fur pelisses -Baying noted the church as a convenient Shelter, they were "making a night of it," with the aid of their plun- der. Some bandsmen had got into the organ loft, andit w4s their performances on the instruments that had caused the melodious sounds whereby Bourgogne and his , friend had been so sorely perplexed.. Others had torn down the woodwork to make a fire, using, among other materials, some of the stairs to the organ-loft, whereby one of the unlucky bandsmen, waking from a drunken sleep by the organ, and attempting to descend," got a fall wh ch incapacitated him from marching for some time. Probably he never came home." 'I he whole some in one of the grimmest, not to say gruesomest, Hogarthian humour. —Front "The Retreat from Moscow," in the " Corn/cell Magazine." THE. CUBAN MACHETE.

_ Much has been said of the terrible machete, a deadly weapon indeed in the hands of a desperate man, and when used against a defenst-less person. The machete was never intended for a weapon of warfare; it is an in- strument of husbandry carried by the Cuban peasant in times-ef peace, and is his one familiar daily companion. it cuts his fire-wood, aids him in building his hut, hews his a h'reo machete weahicththe a ° h te n sariodt n a geuna or straight, 'a nbd ha performs handle,v many a having ing no other ) blade about two an man. The Cuban 9 unsuited as a weapon uh of course, by reason of his long familiarity with the in- strument, is an adept in its use, ttg ofl ju b cpreedf:euth e bug,tT ocd o n "cl ff aT ceontitl end its eact upon a group of unarmed workmen is truly terrible. It is in uil eti t wilitt n the foray against the defenseless and unarmed that the most serious work of the machete has been done in the island of Cun, —"Century." TEE GREATEST ELEMENT OF SUCCESS IN TENNIS-PLYING, Any form of ball-playing will help the beginner to judge the flight of a tennis-ball through the air, and to estimate the is and distance of its rebound from Hi, ground, while merely skipping a rope will teach a girl to j'idge distance and speed. Ole of the greatest ele- ments of success in lawn-tentvs is this ability to judge speed, distance, and angles ; and it is a quality that is not born in one, hut secured only through long training of the eye be constant practice and close observation. Ls the ball flies swiftly towards you, you have only a second or two in which to guess where it will strike the ground, and how far and how Mei; it will bound. Be- fore you can bacoma an expert player, you must be able to estimate to within a few inches the spot a bill will strike, and to within a small fraction of a second of the time it will take to reach an imaginary point in the air after it has bounded, CO that the racket may meet it at exactly the right time and place. I remember hearing Goodbody, the famous English expert, who played in America several years ago, say, one day, that he was feeling in perfect condition for a match. " I believe I could hit a sixpence at the far end of the court," he said And I have seen Wrenn, the American champion, look at a falling ball, and, while it was still high above his head, call" Outside I" and walk away towards the net with perfect confidence in his judgment. When the ball had struck the ground, the umpire declared it to he nut hut not more than six or eight inches. J. Parmly Facet on " Lawn Tennis for School Boys" in" St. Nicholas." THE HUMOURS OF SCARBOROUGH.

I " The queen of watering-places holds her court at Scarborough, and, consequently, the place and the I people plume themselves to no small degree. The core- of the court is somewhat onerous, particularly to the fair sex. Court dress as understood at St. James's is optional, hut court dress as known at Searborowsh is abso'utely indispensable if you would join the select throng in the Spa, Oriental monarchs used to boast of their changes of raiment,lbut the habitues of Scarborough Spa could give them points and win easily. At a non- fashionable seaside resort one's dress need not be changed logarithms in the than six times each day. At the Spa, however, ith certain rules must be observed, and the number of cos- tumes worn by iltass A the course is se of onlyregoll obtained the original idea for his obnee and computedt he w ga,t celebrated e welllde abyrkacnt can id w nquick-change F entertainment by visiting the Spa. He went there every day for a week and learned his lesson well. Of course, the Spa patrons were jealous that be should make money while they exhibited themselves gratuit- ously ; but no one can blame Fregdi. Scarborough, however, does not consist solely of the Spa, and it has other attractions beyond the church parade. This latter, by the way, is the most gorgeous affair of the kind in England, besides which the feeble attempts at Hyde Park, Brighton, and Eastbourne seem puerile There is no other holiday resort where CO many donkeys can be found. The tedious details of court life can be pleasantly varied by a donkey ride for a couple of miles to Scalby Mill. The animals perform each Journey in record time. The preparations for the start are so dilatory, and the movement so imperceptible, that it is hard to tell if you have really started. This absence of Pace is maintained for the whole of the outward Journey, and friends accompanying on foot have ample opportunity for a little fishing, or eVen a bathe, with no fear of being left behind. We suspect these donkeys of a long life, for, as Tom Hood pointed out, 4 Death only wars on the quick/ At Scalby Mill. tea and other refreshment can be had, and • Scalby cakes' are always in demand. For returning to Scarborough let me implore the inexperienced to be circumspect. It is as well for two or three men to hold in the donkey while you mount, then take a deep breath, sufficient to last you for two miles, and wave your hand for the men to let go. I can undertake to say the quadruped will do the return journey inside of five minutes. He may or may not find a person clinging to his back when he reaches Scarborough—usually his saddle is emp`y."— Wilfred Kliclonann in the" Windsor." THE FIRST USE OF FIELD MUSIC. The first use of field music of which we have absolu- tely authentic information was at the battle of Bouvines, that village of French Flanders where the French have won no fewer than three victories—Philip Augustus de- feating Otto IV. of Germany there in 1214, Philip of Valois defeating the English there in 1340, while in 1794 the French defeated the Austrians at the same plate. It was at Bouvines, in 1214, that trumpets sounded the signal for the victorious French charge, the first authen- tic instanee of a'command given by a trumpet call.— Gustave Kobbg in the" Century."

WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
REV. H. PRICE HUGHES pN FOUR
MENACING SIGNS.

The Wesleyan" Conference in its representative session, consisting of 240 ministers and 240 laymen elected by the various district smile throughout British Method- ism, assembled on Monday morning in Great Thornton. street Chapel, Hull, the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes in the chair. The presideet, in welcoming the lay representatives,' said he believed lay representation was the only antidote to desolating clericaliam. There were many special and ardent reasons for the most able co-operation past now between the ministers and people, and to occupy a brief time he would do little more than name what seemed to him the fonr menacing signs of the times which they must frankly face and grapple! with. 1. First ot all there was the idolatry of those physical amusements which had ceased to be a recreation, and whigh had become an insane passion. 2. The constant attacks upon the sacredness of the Lord's Day. Almost the whole Press of this country had been totally blinded and misled by generous but groundless sentiment. He coubi say from personal observation that museums and art galleries were only visited on Sundays by a few thou- sands of the six millions in Landon, and this handful of people consisted almost exclusively of eccentrics and fon, ignore, and those youths and boys who were neither b iya nor men, and whom people usually called "hobble- dehoys." There was also another great evil in London; that was the increase of secular concerts, which were really for profit, on the Lord's Day. 3. The third great evil was the appalling power of the liquor trade. Lord Roeebarry spoke wisely and well when he said that England must control the liquor trade or the liquor trade would control England. 4. Lastly t ley were confronted with the 'nest daring aggressive Bomanism, the last and most incredible demand being for the establishment at the public' I expense of a Roman Catholic University for Ireland. Be leould assure their Irish brethren that they would stand shoulder to shoulder with them to resist this most monstrous injustice. All Romanist nations were going down ; all Pietestant nations were going up. God had committed to the Anglo-Celtic people the defence of human freedom, the vindication of the rights of con- science, the protection of the weak, and the propaga- tion of scriptural Christianity. But all their resourses and all their power were vain and dissolved unless they themselves became better Christians. The president welcomed Bishop Fowler and Dr. Hamilton, who are attending the conference as repre- sentatives from the Methodist Episcopal Church of America. It was unanimously resolved to hold the conference of 1899 in London at Weslev'e Chapel, City-road, to com- mence on Tuesday, July 18th: Mr. R. W. Perks, at P., submitted a resolution to the effect that it was desirable to raise a commemoration fund of one million guineas, to be applied to the exten- sion of the work of God at home and abroad, and that an inflaential committee be appointed to consider this proposal. He hoped that none of the money would go to endowments. Endowments did not strengthen, but rather weakened a Church. (Hear, beer.) He thought it would be wise to place £300,000 at the disposal of some reliable body, like the General Chapel Com- mittee, for providing chapels and central mission halls. The sum of £20,000 should be devoted to educational purposes. There were hundreds of villages where Ang- lican influences were at work to crush out Methodism. He would give £lOO,OOO to foreien missions,and another £lOO,OOO to home missions. He thought that £50,000 should be appropriated in support of Dr. Stephenson's scheme for the removal of Methodist pauper children from workhouses, whilst £250,000 might well be ex- pended in the erection of a Wesleyan Methodist Church House seitable to the present day needs of Methodism, and which should be of a monumental character, built in a central position, not far from Charing-cross. The resolution was adopted, and an influental com- mittee was appointed.

Nearly the whole of the morning session at the Wes. leyan Conference at Hull on Tuesday was occupied with an animated debate on the recommendatioes of the Special Committee on the order of the Conference sessions. Amongst those who t eok a leading pare in the discussion in favour of the suggested change were the Rev. Albert Clayton, Messrs. William Butterworth (Holmfirth), W. Howell Davies (Bristol), Dr. Nicholas (Dublin), and his Honour Judge Waddy. Speaking against the recommendations were Dr. Rigg, Dr. Bowden, of Bath, and Mr. T. G. Osborne, of Colwyn Bay. Ultimately a vote was taken on a resolution as follows :—Having carefully considered the proposals for meeting the difficulties stated to exist in the present arrangement of Conference s,essions, the Conference decides that no more modification of the business of the Conference with a view to seve time will meet the requirements of the case, and that a chance in theiorder of:the sessions is desirable." In favour of this resolution there were 305, and against 110. The Rev. Albert Clayton moved : (1) Thet the decision of the representative Conference on the reversal of the order of sessions be communicated to the pastoral session of the present Conference—agreed ; (2) that the method of electing the president and secretary and the filling up of the Legal Hundred be left to tho pastoral Conference —agreed; (3) that a committee be appointed to censider the recommendations and ?decisions of the district synod in May on the whole question—agreed. Just before Conference rose elections to the depart- ments of the children's, homeeand foreign missionary secretariat were taken. For the former the Rev. Arthur Gregory was nominated to the first place, A. Shareley second, and F. C3wl third. For the office of missionary secretary, in place of the Rev, Mr. Barber, the Rev. William Perkins secured first place,Samuel Todd second, and James Lewis third. In this order the names will be presented to the pastoral session. The voting between the erg two was very close, 138 and 124 being the numbers after the second ballot. During the dinner hour the governors of the Leys Schools, Cambridge, gave a luncheon to many members of the Conference. The table being cleared, Sir James Reckitt said he rejoiced ia the pure Protestant character of the Leys Schools. Mr. Percy W. Bunting said they had had a successful career in the past. Towards the £30,000 required for the relief of the debt on Leys School £5,000 toad been subscribed by old LeYsi'll" themselves. A total of £20,000 would they believed, soon be forthcoming. Their magnificent friend Mr. Waller had sent them £5,000, and that day he had received £250 from an an- onymous donor. Mr. M'Arthur. an old Leyslan. having spoken and promised £5O. Mr. Ferens, j.pe (Hull), wished the scheme all success, and promised £lOO. The proceedings then terminated.

WYCLIFFE P. S. A. SOCIETY. There was a moderate attendance at the service in connection with this society on Sunday. Mr. J. Ker- shaw presided, and in a brief address spoke of Jesus as an example to His followers to use every opportunity to do acts of kindness to all around them. Mr. M. Gosling of Manchester, was the speaker, and he took for his sub- ject " The spirit of helpfulness." Ha contended that the life of a Christian should be distinct, and conspicuous in its purity, and helpfulness. The address was highly appreciated. Mr. W. H. Wallington sang as a solo, " Behold I stand at the door," in a very efficient manner. Mr. T. Parkes, and gr. B. Farrar, also took part in the service.

A NEW MACHINE TO REGISTER HIS DISTANCES.

If the ambition of the Indicator Manufacturing Corn- • pany ba realised, disputes with cabmen about fares will become things of the past. The indicator is intended to act as a safeguard to unsuspezting "fares." It is worked by means of a " cam" fixed to the axle of the wheel. At each revolutien of the la.:ter tho thick pie nf the " ..cam " comes into contact with the piston of a pneu- matic pump. By this means a email quantity of air is forced through a tube into an elastic air chamber, this chamber being contained inside of the meter itself. At each pressure of air the hand on the dial facing the pas- senger indicates the fraction of a mils which the wheel has nogotiated during one revolution. This operation is continued until one mile has been passed, when the indicator is found ta have completed the circuit of the dial once, and the figure " 1 " is displayed on the dial's surface. Any numbor ef miles is thus registered,according to the registering capability of the machine. The company hopes,wherr the machine is brought out, that the licensing authorities will ineist upon every cabman having one fixed to his cab before his license is granted. The actual fares due at the end of each journey will not be displayed on the machines designed for the use of London cabs ; bat for those in- tended for provincial work an ingenious contrivance has seen arranged, which, in addition to showing the dis- tances, will indicate the amount to be paid. It will also enable the cab proprietor to see at the end of a day the exact amount earned by his driver. Yet another machine is to be provided for the ilia of private indi- viduals who drive their own carriages, and who may be desirous of knowing how far they travel during any given time. Its registering capabilities will be for any distance up to a thousand miles. These meters are in- tended to be applicable to any style of vehicle,difference in the sizes of the latter being merely a matter for regu- lation when the machine is fixed.

There was a meeting in Manchester on Saturday after- noon to consider the question of forming a South-East Lancashire League in connection with the above union. It emanated from clubs in the second competition who wanted some attraction to fill in fixtures outside the ordinary tourney Birkenhead Wanderers was one of the clubs convened in the circular, and Mr. Love attended on their behalf A Ion.; discussion ensued, and ultimately the Birkenhead representative said that unless the ordinary competion fixtures could count also as havtng been played in the proposed league his club would not enter He contended that his club could not afford to forego matches against senior clubs like War-. rington, Runcorn and one or two others he hoped to arrange, which they would have to do unless his sug- gestion was agreed to Ultimately, Mr. Lo e was asked to retire, and after discussion it was decided that the Birkenhead Wanderers' proposal could not be ac- cepted,and a league was formed with nit them. The Wan- derers' programme for the coming season will, there- ' fore consist of second competition matches and outside fl tires with such senior clubs as can be arranged with,

div.head: LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.

At a meeting of the committes of the ab3ve competi-. Hon, held in Manch( ster on Tuesday night, the follow- ing impi4rtant bye-law was passed :—" A breach of the professional rules shall have two points deducted from the club's score." A long discussion maned as to the advisability of fixing a minimum charge of sixpence tor all compet:tion matches, but most of the representatives were oppo,ted to the proposal, and ultimately it was de- cided nct t 3 take any actbn in the matter. LANCASHIRE JUNIOR LEAGUE. • The annual general meeting of the League was held at the Spread Eigle Hotel, Manchester, officers for the season being elected as follows :—President, Mr. J Platt; vice-president, Mr. J. Warren; •ecretaries—East Section: H Davies, (Flixton), West Section, A Abe (Ruaccrn). The clubs elected t , constitute the League are :—East Section : Oldnam Juniors, Abbey Hails, Lees, Salford, St. Bartholomew's, R adcliff:3 Hornets, Flixton, Poplar Grove, Brouzlaton Recreation, Altrincham "A," Glenary Hornets, and Hazel Grove. West Section : Runcorn Recreation, Widnes Rangers, Latchford Ringers,B rken- head Wanderers" A," Warrington St. Mary's, Lostock ' Gralarn, St. Elelens " A," Widnes Wilite Star, Fieccher Russell (Warringtoq), and Tanhouse Lane (Widnes). A sub-contimiaeo consisting of tbree from each section was appointed to revise the ralre. WIDNES. The Widnes Football Club are reported to be already practising for the coming season, and have a promising number of players to choose from.

ST. PAUL'S BELLRINGERS AT FARNWORTH.

On Saturday at Farnwerth Church, by kind per— mission of the Vicar, the Warrington St, Paul's ringers, rang a true peal of 5,040 changes in minor methods in 2 haws 54 minutes, consisting of seven 7205.0 f the following methods:—Oxford Treble Bob.. Bent Treble Bob, College Single, Granosire, Oxford Single Bob, Canterbury Plsausure, and Plain Bob. The ringers were as fellows:—Treble, J. J. Wilson; 2nd, Walter Oxley: 3rd, Albert Oxley; 4.h, Edward Edwardson ; sth, William Brammer • tenor, F. W. Stout; and F.W. Stout officiated asconductor. This is the first peal of 5,040 changes by the above ringers as a bend; and the first on the Paraworth church bells.

JUIN 29th, 1898,

Sranr and the United States Peace in have each had enough fighting, Stgbc. and perhaps the division of honours is less unequal than had been at one time foreshadowed. The point, however, is less as to courage and skill in fighting than as to the arrangement of a now basis. If it can be arranged licvir the advantage will be for Spain, because the u:t ere the war is prolonged the more territory Spainraust lose. The war has shown that Spain fi.ght better on land than on sea, though in the she must have been beaten as severely on the '81" 48 she has been on the second. It is very ,sbatural that the good offices of France should be vreferred to the intervention of this country, be- cause Prance has been very sympathetic ; and it Will be said of this country that its attltude has been markc,d by a disposition to see most things with the eyes of Americans. There ri.,as always been in this country a strong uesira to see Cuba better governed and more contented. It has at times amounted to some- thing going beyond a platonic feeling, as, indeed, U 5 s been the case in the United States on several beceasions. If, therefore, there was criticism to egin with of the exaggerations of the American ()flow journals, it was never misunderstood in :Pein,where we were immediately blamed for :duga side with America in the most unfriendly Tbe accusation was not just, but we can r wrti to let that pass. What has taken place vesPecting the Philippines must now convince the "Paniards that we have not been hostile, because there is reason to believe that our representations have coincided with those of other European l'owers, and that Admiral DEWEY has stayed his hand lest he should raise some very dangerous questions. The outlines of the coming peace be- gin to appear in the general haze of the situation. The Philippines are to remain under the sovereignty of Spain. This decision may almost be regarded as the most certain element of the situation. The American papers blame the %ratans for acting against American interests. i/cire have always contended that acting in the ,hilippines was a mistake. Events have now 'ensonstrated the fact. The Guam Islands and a eealing station in the Pacific will represent the Irttnost the Americans can hope to gain in that region. These acquisitions will not violently dis- turb the balance of powers and interests in the Far s-st. Porto Rico and Cuba will pass out of ?Pain's control. It looks as if the former were to °EI annexed by America and made into the site of tile, guardian naval station for that Power in the `-;aribbean Sea. Cuba is to become independent, but the nature and conditions of that independence be la be decided offhand. There is, we hope, to is too hing in the form of a war indemnity. Spain An. per to pay over money to America, and .: erica is too rich to demand it, France should tersfere have by no means a difficult task to s'.range the terms of a satisfactory peace. The LParlish are proud and obstinate, but they are 7aPpily convinced of the bad policy of continuing "War in which they are unable to make an effective ,rte fence, and every engagement brings out some !ell h defects, if it impresses us with the pluck of 051 fighting with poor means against desperate edds.
