They "en treat as novel the policy of making our Navy t‘t(itl:l4l to that of any two European Powsrs,though t Policy was clearly stated seven or eight years is. 7. It is now clear that the cry about our sup- - elll4oy on the sea being an obsolete story has 1,11- 434 d. That is the first thing we have gained. r' Point is one of great importance to us in the 'eral trend of international politics. We not afford to drop behind, orb allow anyone °sincerely doubt our intentions to maintain the til)c)ition we had acquired and our Empire o;e4seltated. On this matter there is no difference °Pinion between Liberals and Consorvatives,and 4tsa Socialists must concede that our commerce t4142.1:1 our food supplies would be imperilled unless 414 supremacy at sea were decisively uph aid. second point gained is that our powers of cltillick augmentation, by reason of our wealth and abundant shipbuilding facilities, are recog- i'eaed anew. When we come to some special and 414Porary views, provoked by Mr. GOSCHEN'S re- of Friday, there is rather more eccentricity Il_erPression. At present we have nothing of tiluto from Russia, where the journals are slow to 4 °l'e,insufficiently supplied with telegraphic news tld tinder so rigorous a Press censorship that ' can be said which is not agreeable to the at,either becau.e its views are embodied ideas it wishes to be current are dissemin- tut the intimation that the Russian pro- been arrested is intended to crest ipression that this country has been forced

kite expenditure by Russian action. The German papers seem to anticipate that Russia will not relish the augmentation,and that, as Mr. GOSCHEA has declared, it is a direct reply to Russia's policy in the Far East—naval, military, and com- mercial. The French papers are not quite sure whether the new programme is directed against Russia or France, or both; but they seem to be rather uneasy about it. Two points come out very distinctly, however, and they are worth notice. The first is that "a senseless pro- gression in naval and military outlay" is said to be a pernicious policy. But it is German,it is French, it is Russian, and it is not necessarily British. We are but taking parallel action, conservative and precautionary in character. The second point isl that a new naval Power has arisen in the world— that of the United States—and that hence England is bound to take it into account in preserving her naval supremacy. In any case,we are hardly to be blamed for doing what we regard as necessary,and the policy does net seem to have created alarm. It is not directed against any settlement of affairs in which the general interests of the world would suffer. Our Far East ern policy is not one of ex- clusive privilege. What we have now to hope for is that Lord Salisbury will not make naval increase the sum and substance of his Policy. That would be a game of bluff. He must take our naval augmentation into account when it is necessary to be bold and decisive, and to put his foot down and keep it there. Otherwise,the next stage of affairs will be worse than the last.

The Goverryneut has lost another seat ! staggering blow has been delivered by the electors of Reading in the return of Mr. Palmer by a ma- ority of 694 over Mr. Kayser, the Conservative candidate. At the general election Mr. Palmer was defeated by 351 votes, and the voting in tho pre- sent contest having been split by the candidature of a Socialist, his success is all the more re- markable and Aisturbing to the party in power. Reading,from its proximity to the capital,—has or previously had—unmistakeable Conservative lean- ings, so that the friends of Mr. Keyser were quite assured of the fitness of fighting the battle round the rock of Goveinmental policy, and parti- cularly Lord Salisbury's foreign policy. On the other hand Mr. Palmer's supporters stood firmly by their guns and advocated the complete Liberal programme. Thus the contest was primarily a trial of political strength, from which, as we have seen, might emerged defeated and right triumphant, if the simile may ho allowed. The Government Party, in the light of history, viewed the aspirations of the Socialist nominee with great satisfaction, be: .

lieving that the votes recorded in his favour would just about turn the scale against their opponent. But they under-estimated the disfavour which the Government has fallen into, and Mr. Palmer has swept the board in decisive fashion, obtaining the heaviest vote ever polled in the constituency in • spite of the three-cornered nature of the fight. Much more evidence of a retrospective and com- parative kind might be adduced, but it is unneJes- sary. The point, patent to all, and unpleasantly clear to the Government, is that the weakness, in- firmity, and incapacity of the present session has rendered a great Liberal triumph not only certain, but imminent.

The numerous grave charges against medical me i' of considerable social and professional stand- ing, has had a disquieting effect. It appears quite evident that certain mid-practices of a criminal nature are not only committed with frequency, but their detection is to a large extent impossible unless the issue is fatal to some unfortunate person. Since the Collins case there has been quite a crop of prosecutions against surgeons for similar dangerous and illegal practices. The exposure of these scandals, combined with the punishment of the guilty persons, may have their good effect, and it is comforting to be able to view these painful cases from such a standpoint. If the members of such an honourable and benefi- cent profession as that of medicine,—those of them at any rate who are not above abusing it—can be brought to realise the gravity of their offence and its probable unpleasant se.quel,the number of such unsavoury scandals will be greatly reduced, and perhaps put a stop to. The unpleasantness of the antidote would be speedily forgotten if the source of trouble could be so remove.

Mr. Hooley's long expected revelations have not proved so sensational as was anticipated, so far as the charges against the press are concerned. The only question is whether, having regard to the blast of trumpets b 3forehand, Mr. ''Hooley has been as absolutely frank and full in his disclosures as it was possible for him to be. So far as the "Pall Mall Gazette" is concerned the editor and proprietors appear to be more entitled to sym- pathy than to blame. Whatever may have hap- pened was done without their knowledge,and they cannot be held culpable for it. The other princi- cipal payment alleged was in respect of a compara- tively small financial paper, and as the person whose name was mentioned is now undergoing impriswinvent, and the paper has changed hands, this canlaut be said to be at all a wonder-working bit of news. The Press, indeed,has reason to com- plain that Mr. Hooley should have maligned it so broaally, and have left the accusation as a cloud over the heads of all, instead of specifying more 1 clearly the causes of his complaint. But the aristocrats who were the ornamental figure-heads with which Mr. Hooley worked do not come out so satisfactorily. The public will put a diminishing value on such recommendations when they learn that the Earl De La Warr received £50,000 for his trouble as a director, half of which he had to pass over to other persons for what they had done. The Duke of Somerset stands out with conspicuous honour, but the arithmetic of the Earl of Albe- marle seems to have been so faulty as to have made it clear that he was chosen for his name and not for his business ability. Once more the lesson is enforced that mere names should count for no- thing with investors.

The painful surprise with which many Socialists appear to have received the intelligence of the pecuniary condition of Dr. Pankhurst at the time cf his death will doubtless result in the collection of a suf&ient sum of money to place the widow and children beyond the reach of want. Dr.Panh- hurst in his later years devoted his best energies to Socialism. He seems to have been looked upon as a man of means, but all the while his political tenets were damaging his practice and taking away hia means of living. But his Socialism was sincere. He preached it with what fervour he could, and left the future of himself and his family to fortune. His case raises anew an old ethical ' problem which can never be satisfactorily answered, so far as high thinkers are concerned, though it presents very few difficulties to the im- mense majority of people who are content to be merely practical. How far is a man justified in sacrificing his wife and children to his political or moral principles ? If such principles are taken seriously, and if, at the same time, the man is deeply religious, his answer will probably be that he must sacrifice his family unblenchingly, fear- lessly leaving their future in the hands of that Providence which has endowed him with so severe a conception ef duty. To carry out views of that kind is a task of no little bitterness,and to some its successful consummation may seem to elevate the idealist to a nobility not often reached by frail humanity. Practical people, as we have said, are content to look to the safety of their wives and I children first ; their principles are things to be nibbled at during the performance of that first duty, and fully adhered to only when it has been entirely accomplished.

Very much on the same principal as "one man one vote--one Methodist one guinea—the Wesle- yan body is going to inaugurate the opening of the twentieth century. Mr. R. W. Perks' great Million Guinea Scheme has been enthusiastically adopted,and between January 15t,1899 and January Ist, 1900, the sum of o e 4.linea will be required

from at least one million Wesleyans. We confi- dently anticipate the success of this magnificent effort for the propagation of the Gospel in the first place, and the sustenance and expansion of Wesle- yan Methodism, in the second place. Methodists, though individually far from wealthy, have always skown the most praiseworthy willingness to part with their substance as a guarantee of the sincer- ity of their religious convictions. And while to many, a guinea is a big sum and one that cannot be spared from the household exchequer, yet even such will be found aiding the project with smaller donations,or work- ing hard to collect the stipulated subscription. The" million " is to be disbursed through the best of channels, viz :—Assisting the erection of Wes- leyan Methodist places of worship, educational work and the combating of Romanism in rural dis- tricts, home and foreign missionary work, and the purchase of a site for the subsoquent erection in London of a connexional building. The latter pro- ject will absorb a quarter of a million pounds, and for this sum we think a building compatible even with the dimensions, and worth of the Wesleyan body might comfortably be erected. Daring the forthcoming eighteen months therefore, the chief subject to exercise the Methodist mind will be the provision of that guinea, and with such a period to "save up " in, added to their characteristic generosity, we see no reason small or great why the Million Guinea Scheme should not be an unqualified success, and a triumph for the Metho- dist cause.

To the reader in search of " light" reading we can hardly mem-am-mid the bulky volume contain- ing the annual statement of accounts by the Borough Treasurer which has been issued this week, but still the book contains information which should be interesting to ratepayers. The long-suffering ratepayer who wishes to see how much his representatives have spent on deputa- tions has only to peer through some one hundred Pacres in order to acquaint himself with the exact amount. After doing so we believe he will corns to the conclusion that they show no signs of diminishing,for the total daring the twelve months exceeds £l5O. The provision of a new Mayor's parlour has also proved an expensive item. This has cost the ratepayers £27o—a rather large sum considering the necessity there has been for economy in order to keep the rates as near 6s in the £as possible. Even such a small luxury as Mayoral insignia causes the ratepayer some ex- pense. As a matter of fact the uniforms for the mace and sword bearers cost £2O Els, and then there is a further sum of £2 Os 61., for" insurance of Mayoral insiomia." Bat theso are small items when compared with £2ll ss. far caskois and scrolls for freemen of the Borough, and £76 103. for grant of Borough Arms.

The profits made by the Markets Committee, and also on the gas and water undertakings, are pleasinc, items, and show that the Corporation makes money as well as spends it. W:th refer- ence to the -Weights and Measures department we notice that a profit has been made of nearly £lso.This, of couse, has accrned from local trades- men who aro obliged by law to have their weights and measures adjusted from time to time, but it is vary seriously to be questioned whether the Corporation have a right to make a profit out of the undertaking. A more equitable arrangement would appear to be to reduce the charges which are made for the duty involved. From the bal- ance sheet which accompanies the accounts it appears that there is an excess of assets over liabilities amounting to £277,449 18s. 6d. It will be gratifying to the ratepayers to learn that the Corporation is financially over a quarter of a million to the good, but some of the items in the balance statements are very vague, and seem to require a little elucidation. For instance of what value to the outsider are such items of assets as " street improvements " £41,392 2s. 103., or "property purchased for street improvement purposes £36,861 12s. 1d.,0r again "amount expended on new sewers" £59,580 2s. 91 It would be interesting to know how these amounts have been arrived at, and to what they refer. If the amounts are simply capital outlay then they are not of much value. The amount expended is no guide as to the market- able value of the asset; it might be worth more than the outlay involved or it might be worth very much less.

The proposals for the Gladstone National Me- morial have now beec licked into shape, and the report of the executive received unanimous con- firmation at a meeting of the general committee last week. In the first place, as was indicated at the earlier proceedings of the committee, the ob- ject is primarily "to establish a memorial to Mr Gladstone which shall be personal to him and shared in by all parts of the United Kingdom." The first proposal which has come tol a definite head,is for the erection of a monuments memorial, thetyps of which will be subsequently decided, in the three capitals of England,Scotland, and Ireland.By this arrangement each country will possess a distinct memorial indicative of its own veneration and love for the departed Stqtesman. Then, at Hawarden, a building is to be erected to contain the books of St.Deiniers'Library,collected and shelved by the hands of Mr. Gladstone himself, and which, we trust, will soon be looked upon as a second "Temple of Peace." At his own home there will thus be, in addition to the many evi- dences:o4th° sentiment ofjthe family and villagers,a substantial testimony to the gratitude of a nation. The memorials agreed upon strike us as suitable in most respects. They are, perhaps, scarcely adequate when compared with the phenomenal and touching outburst of sorrowful feeling which immediately followed Mr. Gladstone's death, but as it is intended to uthise by some further memorial scheme what residue of funds there may ultimately be, in the end there will probably be nothing vv inting (to make the National Memorial fulfil the expectations and desires of all well-wishers.

That accidents will happen in the best regu- lated (Royal) families has been made painfully evident by the ordeal to which the Heir-Apparent to the Throne will be subjected for some days to come. The Prince of Wales has reached a period of life when his movements are dictated by the ' caution of a middle-age, hut though he has es- caped in his years of more daring travel and ad- venture any fracture of limb, the misfortune has now come upon him in the simple act of descend- ing the stairs of an old English residence. The incident recalls a similar one that befell Mr. Frederick Whymper, who, after ascending the Great Andes and performing other feats which are recorded in his books,caught his foot on the stairs of a local town hall,where he was about to deliver a lecture on his climbing prowess, and broke his leg. The Prince's injury is apparently confined to a simple fracture,but to so distinguished a per- sonage any illness is very unpleasant, on account of the stir it creates. Moreover, though there is an ignorant belief that the Prince of Wales enjoys the most luxurious leisure, it is very well known to those who read the papers that few public per- sonages are so busy,or can,in a sonse,less afford to be laid by. The Prince is ever ready to support movements for the good of the people by his pre- sence and his absence from public functions of this kind involves a serious loss. Even greater sympathy will be extended to the Prince now that it is reported that he will in all probability have a permanent slight limp.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[Blt A CORRESPONDENT].

What does the London and North Western Rail- way Company benefit from the traffic to and fro over the Runcorn Bridge, in a twelve-month, I wonder? Has anyone ever set to and worked the problem ? If tbey have, then they must have been surprised ?

Putting the number of people that cross the bridge daily at 600, which I believe, is a very low estimate,and after making due allowances for con- tract ticket holders, let us suppose that the com- pany secure 500 threepences daily for six days a week; what does it work out to in a twelve-month? Why just about £3OO short of £lO.OOO a year, assuming that the extra £3OO is made up by the passengers that cross the line by ordinary train, we have the round sum annually, of £lO,OOO accruing from bridge tolls. Further putting the cost of maintenance at say one half; £5,000 clearly comes out of the people's pockets. Some 600 people pay about .£8 6s. 8.1. annually in bridge money.

This is a fabulous amount to pay annually for a promenade ! In pointing out these things I wonder however they came abcut. Why any private com- pany would consider themselves well-paid if they erected a swing footbridge (Acts of Parliament and all thrown in) and worked it at a penny-a-head. Indeed, it would be a safe 10 per cent investment Now baying shown there is money in it, I will pro ceed a stage.

The Corporation of Widnes is rich : the Corpora- tion of Runcorn i.e., (Urban District Council) is not so very poor —at any rate they are not above spend- ing a little money for value. Now if these two could come to a concerted action, and either do something to get', the tolls reduced or else buy over the right of way, they would confer an immense boon on the community. I feel sure—whether they use the bridge or not—that the ratepayers would not object to paying a little extra rate for such a benefit.

Nov you councillors who have your hands full of public baths. electric lighting, cheaper gas, better water, wider streets, fever hospitals, to say nothing of the proposed roadways, dare you tackle this little project ? Or is there a heavy block that prevents your disinterested action such es shares ? If so, take care you 'lna% tall on the edge of your own axe, while grinding it.

Sorns preachers would do well to read what fol- lows:—" Never preach about any•hin,t.Y, you do not understand. If you clearly understand all about your subject you would preach shorter sermons and let your congregation get home to Sunday's dinner and so appreciate a day of rest." Runcorn priests, pastors, ministers, etc., readint. this will benignly smile whilst the thought " It's for the other fellows " flits phantom-like through their brain. Well, Tilly be it is. But long words and unsound dogma won't maks us better Christians. "Ia the multitude of words there lacks wisdom " and (re- vised version) " appetite."

Must I give in to the scheme of public baths to cost I think about £2,500, and which will increase the value of the market so very much. There is the talk of lock-up-shopi which will let at so muchond this that and the other that will bring in so much revenue (all very rosy)and the supporters of the scheme just think that it can be worked with au annual cost of £133 a year. I still think, that the provision of public baths had better have catered for as men;ioned bsfore, along with the Heath and Common undertaking. There is no necessity to have the very best baths in the world, bat an attraction will be required to set off the Heath and Common. Therefore I submt what be,ter attraction could there be than a good bath, the maintenance and keepinz of which could be included in the one account.

If the market is so useless as a market, how has it become so ? Surely not because there is no enter- prising spirit of barter left amongst ti:? No, not for this reason, but because the market hao 108,12 handicapped, and hampered,—boycotted if you like instead nf being widely utilised and facilitated. And I say lithe conversion is made there will be a cry for a Market raised in a short time. Upon the man- agement of the Market there is cast a reflection in the bare suggestion of its abolition, Let our time- honoured, though much vilified Marmot remain a market. Certainly we want baths—l am an advo- cate of the bath—bet don't deprive Us of an insti- tution which has had its rise and fall with our own.

div.head: KNIFING TEE POLICE AT FRODSHANE
div.p: KNIFING TEE POLICE AT FRODSHANE
PRISONER SENI. To GIOL

01 Wednesday at the S sssions House,Frodsham,beEere Mesirs, Charles Reynolds, and W. Timmins. John fl -rose. of Wood Flouses, Frodsham, wn.q brought aro in custedy charged on three separate counts. Viz : Ttriink and disorderly on the 23 July ; drunk and and refusing to quit licensed wornisea on the 25th of July ; and with assaalting P C Bebbinzton, whits'. in the execution of hia duty.—Prisoner pleaded guilty to the two first charges. but denied knowledge of the latter. P.C. Bebbington said about 12 noon on the 25-11 of this month he was called into the " Wh tlebons '' Inn, to eject the prisoner. He became very violent and used I bad language. Consequently witness had to take him in charge. 11rhen he got outside, prisoner aimed a blow at witness, but he warded it off. He then noticed that the prisoner had an open knife (produced) in his hand and that he had cut through his (witness's) jaekst and waistcnat.and only for the buti-on of his braces it would probably have boon a serious stab. He did not wish to zharze him,however,with cutting and wounding. Prisoner, who had no questions to ask. said he did not remember anything about the knif 3 until he was told about it. The other charges wore then formally proved. The Chairman: You will be fined 51 inc'uding cnsts, for the case on the 20'h Julr.—For the assault on the constable—(you know you had a knife in your hand, and it is very lucky that the blade got caught).—Yeu will go to gaol for that. Prisoner : I did not know I had the knife in my hand sir. The Chairman : That is nonsense. It would be the same thing if you had killed your man. You will go to gael for 14 days with hard labour. For being drunk and refusing to quit you will be fined 54 and costs or 14 days in default, the sentences to run concurrently.

div.head: PRESENTATIONS TO MR. F. H. GOSSAGE, J,P., AND MR. T. 8. TIMMS, J.P.
div.p: PRESENTATIONS TO MR. F. H. GOSSAGE, J,P., AND MR. T. 8. TIMMS, J.P.

On Wednesday afternoon, at a special meeting of the Widnes Town Council, to which the members of the School Board and the Free Library and Technieal In- struction Committes were invited, held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, the Honorary Freedom of the Borough was conferred upon Mr.F.H. Gossage, J.P., ! and Mr.T. Sutton Titnmis, J.P. There was almost a full attendance of the members of the public bodies named, I and the Mayor(Aldarman J.W. Wareing) presided. The decision to confer the freedom of the borough on these gentlemen was unanimously arrived at by the town council at a special meeting held on the 18'h of January I last, the desire of the council being to recognise the emi- nent public services they have rendered to the town. Mr. Gossage was for 23 yeas a member for the local board prior to the incorporation of the town in 1892, and for ten years was chairman of that body. Be was appointed provisional mayor on incorporation, and at the meeting I of the town council he was appointed mayor, holding ' the office for two years. He was also appointed an Alder- man, and that office be held until last year, when he re- I signed owing to ill-health, his son, Captain W. W. Gos- sage, J.P., being elected to fill the vacancy. Mr. Timmins was elected chairman of Widnes school Board in 1876, and for thirteen years and upwards he rendered in that capacity signal services t 3 the town in carrying into effect the ! Elementary Educet,on Act. Both gentlemen have in other reepect I conferred innumerable benefits upon the town, and the decision of the Council to confer upon them the highest honour in their power was received I with the utmost satisfaction by tee ratepayers. The ! resolutions of the Council conferring the freedom of the bormaeh had been t utefuily inscribed on illuminated scrolls, mounted on ivory rollers, and theae were en- closed in massive silver gilt caskct chastely designed an I executed,bearing the borough and enmity arms.and representations in enamel of the 'Down Hill,the Techni- cal Scheel, St. Paul's Church, and Runcorn Bridge. The caskets are mounted on red plush on ebony stand, and are fine specimens of the goldsmiths' art. Toe Mayor said the duty he was called upon to per- form that afternoon was not only one of the mist im- portant, but it was one of the most pleasurable duties that load fallen to his lot during his occupancy of that chair. He referred in eulogistic terms to the public ser- vices rendered to the town by Mr. Gossage and Mr. Timmia. Both of them were alike distinguished for the eminent services they had rendered to the town, and by their many and varied ace ef munificence towards every object having for its ultimate aim and end the moral, ineePectnal, and ma:erial welfare of the people at large. (Applause.) He regretted that owing to the state of Mr. Gossage.'s health that event had not been held in a larger hall, and at an hour when the general body of the rate- payers could have been present to witness the conferring of these honours upon two of the most worthy and die- tinguished citizens of the borough. (Applause). The Town Clerk then read the resolution of the coon- I cil conferring the freedom of the borough on Mr Gos- ' save, and the Mayor presented the casket to that gentleman, which he loop,d he wou,d consider worthy of I acceptance as a memento of that important and memor- able necasion. (Applause). Mr. Gerage signed his name on the roll of honorary f7teemen of the horouvh, and on rising to acknowledge I the gift was received with lou I applause. He said he was sorry he was not strong enough to make any sort of a speech, but what be did sly he said with all trmilful- loess. His earnest desire was to thank them most heartily for the honour they had conferred upon him. He assured them that he considered the gift the most urecieus one they could confer upon hi:ll,am] he regar- ded the very flittering address and the mest artistic! casket, as a lanutiful expression of their kindly feeling. Indeed he had never reeeived anything but kindness in Widnes, and that was saying a good deal for a resident of 45 years. (Applause). . .

A sirnilar ceremonial wasgone through with regard to Mr. Timmis, and the mayor in orosentirn% the casket and the freadom it contained, said the words he had used with relation to Mt. Gossage &so applied to Mr. Timmins, except that he congratuiated the last-named gentleman noon being in the enjoyment of very good health. (Applause.) Mr. Timrnis also r,ceived a flattering reception on rising to re,pond. He accepted the freedom of the borough, and the elegamt casket in which it was en- shrined, with the greatest pleasure—a pleasure which was very much enhanced by his Worship's gracious words and the terms of the resolution, and of the speeches made when it was unan4mously passed by the Council. (Applause.) But he could not consider him- self deserving of all the good things they had said of him; rather would he attribute them to their good nature than to his cl,serts. However, he was conscious that he had done acme little for the good of the town—(applause) and it was very gratifying to find that what he bad d0n..., had been recognised. (Hear, hear.) Public life was distinctly distast.ful to him; but he was a great admirer of our public instit flier's and the self-goveraing powers developed by our race, which ,4EI regarded as the root of the prosperity and greatness of the country—(applause) —and he had al ways taken the view that any man wt.° had the pow r of being gll2iul in the town where be lived shou'd not, F his fellow-townsmen wished him C under• take public duties, shrink from dis.tharging them; aid it was th.t reasoo, and that reason only, which induced him to leave the business he liked to undertake nubile business which he did not like. Mr. Gossage h-ld the same snows, and considering tht they would ha mor? useful on two bodies than if they worked on one to- gether. they had taken separate lines. He (Mr. Timmis) retir -,el because be thought younger men would to mere useful. ("No, no.") Bet though public werk was done, be hoped to still be (d Born,a rvice to the town in other directions. Opp &Ise.) ne would t,easor a their gift as long as he was spared as oue of his choicest pos• SP,/ 0 is. (Applause.) Toe proceedings then terminated.

The Wesleyan Conference resomed its sitting in Hu 1 on Wednesday morning, tie Rev. H. Price Hughes presiding. On the report of a special committee, it was agreed that the ordinary rotation of ne conferences should be as follows :-1899. London; 1900, Burslem ; 1901, New- castle-on-Tyne; 1902, Mancnester; 1903, Camhorue;l9o4, 4rdßitrir;m 19inlgOt,ia Lmiv;eir9pio4o.lii; u 1911; 111,9P115,-, Sheffield; 1905, Bristol; 1906, No' tmgliam; 1907,Loadon; 1908, Bradford; 1909, (1 mouth; 1912, Leeds; 1913, London. By this arrangement toere will be a. reversion to the old practice of holding t".e conference in London twice as often as in any one provincial t ma. The representative conference endorsed the consent given by the pastoral session to the establishment of an annual assembly for Welsh Methodism. Mr. S:ephenson, London, and Mr. R. W. Perks, M.P., brought up the report of the committee appointed to outline the proposed scheme for rsisiag a million guineas to commemorate the beginning ot the next century. The proposal was received with great enthusiasm, and although varied suggestions were made and considered the scheme was accepted with perfect unanimity, and without a divided vote thr ,ueliout the discussion. Toe treasurers were appointed as follows :—Mr. R. W. Perks, M.P., Mr. Taomas Walker, Holton ; Mr. T. S. Bain- laii :go, Neweastle-on-Tyne ; Sir George J. Smith, Truro ; the Rev. VValford Green; honwary secrrariee, Rev. Dr. Popp, Rev. Dr. Stephenson, Rev. Simpson Johnson, Rev. Rev. F. L. Wiseman, M. P. W. Bunting (Loudon), Sir George H. Chubb (London), Mr. W. Middlebrook (Mor- ley), and Mr. John Barnsley (3.rrnins,,hani). The Rev. Albert Clayton was nominated to the pummel session for appointment as general secretary. When the scheme was finally adopted the coaferenee jeiried in singing the Doxology.

Brighouse, ooroner, held an inquiry into the cirearn• stances attending the death of William Henry Marsh, 26 years of age, a labourer, of 8, Newton Terrace, Earles- town,whose body was recovered from the Sankey Canal on Monday afternoon. From the evidence of the brother Joseph Marsh, it appears I the deceased had lodged with a Mrs. Lane, in Lawrence-street, but having some dis- agreement with one of the daughters he left the house on the 23rd inst. and went to live with his brother in Newton Terrace. He went out on Sunday after partak- ing of his tea and came ia again about a quarter to ten. He again went out and was seen by a man going in . the direction of the canal, and was no: seen again. On Mon- day afternoon his coat and cap were found on toe Earle- street side of the .Ilanal bank near the Ship Ina locks by Thomas rieins, who gave information to the police. In one of the pockets was found a priviligi. ticket order bearing his name. P.C. aspien dragged till canal,and recovered the body ate It six o'clock, mil it was re- moved to the boas. of hie; brother.-1 verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane" was returned.

div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A WARRINGTON WOMAN'S TEGIFTS.-9HAIIP SENTENCE. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Saturday, before Mr. Thomas Birch&lt (in tee chair), Alderman Blackhurst and Mr. Hayward, Elizabeth Humphreys, widow. 49,01 d-road, Latchford, was charged with steal- ing from Se James' Schoel on July Ist a tablecloth value 155., the property of the school authorities, and she was further charged wiih stealing on July 4'h from the shop of E V. Morton, pawnbroker, Latchford, a cotton shirt value is. lld„ and with stealing from St. James' School some time in January last, to dovn tea spoons valued at 23. 6.1., also the property of the St. James' school authorities.—The prisoner pleaded guilty. —The Chief Constable maid the prisoner had been employed by the St. James' Sehool authorities on special occasicn.,such as to parties. On Walking Day she was employed. On the day following a large tablecloth was missed, and the caretaker of the school asked prisoner if she knew anythbeg about it. She replied that she had not seen it. Information of the loss was given to the police, and Detectives Monaghan and Forster made inquiries and found that on the 15th July. a fortnight after the theft, prisoner had pledged a portion of the cloth at the pawnshop of Mr. Morton, Latchford. It was subsequently found that during prisoner's service at the school a number of tea spoons had been stolen, and in- quiries resulted in the discovery that prisoner had also pledged those. When appreheadee, a large number of pawntickets was found in her house, two relating to the . two leentna of tablecloth, another to the spoons, and a fourth to the shirt stolen from the shop of Mr. Morton. Prisoner had gone in the shop to pledge something and whilst there had stolen the shirt from the counter. She " had previously served seven sentences of a month for similar thef r s.—The Chairman described the case as a very serious one, and cammitted prisoner to gaol for - three months hard labour, one month on each charge. THEFTS FROM THE "NEW BOAT EIOI7Se AT WILDERSPOOL. At the Warrington Police Cne.rt, on Monday, before the Mayor (in the chair), and other magistrates, John Carter, or Catb try, was charged with stealing from a tool shed of tae "Now Bost Howie," Wilderspool, a trowel and a pair of boots, the property of James Williams. and a hammer the property of Michael D3oley, and a plane the property of Joseph Jameson.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—Tbe Chief Constable said the prisoner was arrested on three separate charges of steal- ing tools. The workmen were employed on a new build- ing known as the "New Boat HOUSS" in course of erec- tion. They had a tool house, and one of the workmen locked the place up on Saturday afterneon. The key was then hung up in another erection. When the work- men came on Monday morning they found the ki had been taken and the articles were missing from the tool house. It was also found that Mr. Jameson's plaee in Liverpool-road had been entered and a plane had been maieseee—elmes Williams,plasterereiving in Wilderspool- road, and employed on the new heeding, said on Satur- day last the 16th July he placed his boots and tools in the lock-up place. He afterwards missed those articles about 9 o'clock on Monday morning.—Michael Dooley, an apprentice plasterer, also employed on the building said he placed his toos in the place. He missed his lath hammer on Monday morning,it was worth 2a61 —Thomas Horan, 18. Ellesmere-street said on Saturday morning the 16th July he locked up the tool house. Be then put the key in another erection which had an un- glazed window in ft.—Joseph Jameson who was sworn on the New Testament, said the plane was his property. Be believed it was in the office formerly, but it was not in oc Monday morning when he went at 9 o'clock and the office door was open. The plane was stamped with the name of Jameson.—Joseph Ashton an assistant to Mr. E. V. Morton, pawnbroker, said on Saturday the prisoner came to his shop and offered that plane in pledge. Be said his name was Jameson. Witness lent him 91 on it.—Detective Inspector Monaghan said on Saturday last he arrested the prisoner in Manchester. Be was wearing the boots identified, as having been stolen. Witness charged him as he was now charged, and prisoner said he had not taken them but had found them in a new house. He said a man had given him the plane. The nench sent prisoner to prison for 14 days for each char,,e, sir weeks in all.

A San Caen Boger-street, was charged on a warrant with committing an assault upon his wife, Ellen.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant.—The COMplainant, who made a long statement, said key husband bad not been sober since Saturday. When sober he would not speak a word to aoyone. He cam* home at 7-30 on Saturday night and threatened to " Christen her." What this terrible threat meant was not explained, but the nom- plainant evideotly regarded it as a serious one. He subse- quently kicked her and caused her to fall to the fluor saying "now I have served you as I promised vou." She did not wish him "to be sent off," but asked the Bench to grant her a separation order and she would andeevour to , keep herself—ln answer to Mr. Browns she admitted that she did scratch her husband, but she did solo self-defence. because he was drunk. The present was the first time Rho had had occasion to Gammon him.—By the Chairman: She did nothing to aggravate him. He " came into the loons' like a lion let loose out of a den."—ffir. Browne said the defendant bore more wounds than the complainant. Ths dispute arose about a missing half-crown, and it continued throughout Saturday and Sunday. The money wee, how- ever, subsequently discovered. There was no doubt the woman did aggravate her hasband —The Chairman: Women can say nasty and bitter things which it is difficult lons man to stand. Women are not altogether free from fault.—Corn- plainant : I dare say that is so. --The case was adjourned for four weeks, to give the couple an opportunity of settling their differences. gr. John Morris, and Robert Okell. three young men, all described as labourers, and residing in Run- corn, were summoned on the information of Police-Sergeant Gill, for gaming in a public place with cards on the 17:h of July.—ln answer to the charge Robinson and Morris pleaded not guilty, and Okell that he was not playing at all.—Ser- geant Gill said in consequence of numerous complaints received by him of the practice of playing cards in the vicinity of Church street he Was on the watch s and saw a number of young fellows playing or and passing money. He recognised Roblnqon, Morris and Okell. but the rest ran away. He had been watching them for some twenty minutes from his bedroom window.—Cress-examined: Sergeant 081 said he was sure that the defendants were playing cards and passing money, though he saw neither money nor cards when he Came up.—The Bench: Have you the slightest doubt that they were playing cards doubt whatever.—Samuel Boetla called for the defence said he was sitting not far from the defendants, and saw no cards played at all. They were in the box a long, time and playing about, "talking and larking," but not playing cards, and no money* passed. —Superintendeat Ok,ll : Where were yot sitting '—l was sitting near the top of the street, by the coroner. I knew Robinson very well.—Mrs. Price. 36. Nelson-street, called to prove an alibi for Okell said that the boy was with her and her prop's all the time. He only got up at half past twelve and did not go away at all until half-past three.—Superin- tendent Okell: How does that agree with the statement by 1 the boy's mother "that he was not with the other boys but was looking at the Volunteersr—Witness : He oonid not be in two pieces at the same time. and possibly the mother was " taint Iles."—The bench who coniddered the case proved. addressing the defendants said: Roblumn you are an old hand at this sort of thing and have lo,"n fined on a previous occasion 10s. and costs ; you will suffer the same penalty this time, which is taking a very lenient view of the case. div.head: ODD-FELLOWSHIP.
div.p: ODD-FELLOWSHIP.
P.G.M. GRAHAM ON SPLIT-AIDED PENSIONS.
The half-yearly meeting of the Parton Dicariet, M. U.• wag held at the Shoulder of Mutton lon, B irton-undur- Nee d mood.

_ . P.G.M. Graham said that Burton had taken part in the important question of State-aided pensions since 1885. He gave a vestion of the history since that time, aud brought it down t what was done at Douglas whs the Burton and several other Propositions were referred to the next A.M.C., that being, as they knew. held at Oxford last Whit-week. Oa the main principle a, Bristol they had a majority of 47—on a total vote of 534 —and that resolution had never been challenged. • At the Bristol AM C. in 1898„ there was a conference, a-, which 15 districts interested in the matter were repro seated. Then the cernpliment was paid to Burton to voice the whole of the districts in regard to State- aided pensions,and their proposition, as he had Reid, was carriei, with the addition *arced to from North London. At the Douglas A.M.C., 1897, the'whole question was referred to the Oxford A.M.C., and here again there was a conference of delegates from districts interested, and it was decided to proceed only with the Wrinehill pro- position, which did not deal with State-aid at all, that question having been settled at Bristol. They purpasely avoided that, until they ware challenged from the other side. What they wanted was an expression of opiiiien as to whether the officials of the Order, and especially the Grind Master for the time being, should be permitted to talk against State-aided pensions in public, unless the Bristol vote was reversed, and that vote, he felt positive, would never be changed. He then proeeeded to disegree with the action taken by Grand Master Turner, and especitlly alluded to his correspondence with the Registrar of Friendly Societies. We did all we could to further the liberty of speech view, for there seemed to be au attempt to gag speakers who were in favour of State-aid, and he emphatically objected to any attempt at gagging. The proposition sub- mitted from Wrinehill read as follows when , amended by N irth London and accepted by Wrinehill:—" Seeing that the Bristol A.M.C. adopted a , resolution pledging the M.U. to give its cordial support to any vvell-cens,derecl and suitable scheme propounded by the Legislature for the relief of the aged and infirm, benelitting our unfortunate brethren, provided th ,t the pension is independent of the poor law, and does no create any power of interf srencs in the general manaea ment of the Order, this A.M.C. trusts that any official, when acting in his official capacity, will not do any- thing of a nature contrary to the spirit of the said reso- lution." For the proposition as amended, 241; egaintt. 301. That proposition he rejeicod to see lost, rind con- tended that the Bristol decision stood exactly where it originally did, and that no one dare really challenge it. That proposition was for State-aid without Sate interference, and he believed t iat the vast naajerit of memberf of the Order were ie favour of that. He hoped that next Christmas a prop ositionoimilar to that Mt to Oxford to Burton,erould be sent to the next A.M.C. The only answers they got at Oxford were personalities, and he protested against that line of conduct. The statements oneht tv have been met with sound arguments on the real question of procedure, but the debate had been allowed to drift. There was, however, a glorious future dawning for them. The future Grand Master wte in their favour, with freedom of speech.and Burtoe which had been in the forefront since 1885 on this question, would no doubt again bring forward tee mater, and persevere until they had accomplished the object they had in view. In reply to a question, he added that the Registrar of Friendly Societies would never dictate to them. He was their faithful servant, and because the A.M.C. passed the proposition for State- aided pensions it would have to be incorporated in the rules and the Act amended, before it could corn, into operatioe.

His method has been to sell imitations of Hood's Sarsa- pa,illa and other well known medicines at absurdly low prices, leading the people to believe they were gettirg g,eat bargains.—ln the Chancery Court of Lancashi e, at Manchester, before Vice•Chaticellor Hall, the plaintiff's were represented by Mr. Grant, and the defendant appeared in person and submitted to a perpetual injunction, restraining him from passing or his goods as being of plaintiff's manufacture.—The lesson from the incident is that people should seve buy Hood's Sarasparilla Or other medicine of hawkers. pedlars, or auctioneeis, but should purchase only of , reliable chemists or prtent medicine vendors, win will supply just what is cilled for. •

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MISS BERTHA GHEENA.LL.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS BERTHA GHEENA.LL.

The little village of Wall,ou,which is at any time, even when wearing its every-day aspect, exceed- ingly pretty, Presented an unusually charming appearance on Tuesday afternoon. The villagers, who of late have had ample practice in the art of dressing the village in gay colours, succeeded ad- mirably in their plea4ing duty on the occasion of the marriage celebration of Miss Bertha Greenall, daughter of the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., ot Walton Hall, to Ai r. i ward Waldegrave Griffith, only eon of Captain Griffith, of Tarporley. Beauti- fully fine weather favoured the event. The sun shone with great brilliancy on the bright dresses of the ladies gathered in front of the church and lower down the read,who had come to view the interest- ing scene. Coming from Warrington the first thing which would catch the eye was a large arch erected close to the church by Mr. Joseph Sluskett's work- men. The structure was draped in a most artistic manner and stretched right across the road. on the one side was the motto " Health, happiness, and prosperity," and on the reverse side " May every blessing, attend you." On the top of the arch a shield was fixed bearing the crest of the Greenall family, three bu,les with a bloody hand, and on either side of the arch shields were fixed with the family snotto—Alta l'eto(I wish to rise) on one side, and on the other the initials of the bridegroom I E. W. G. The villagers had also done their share in the decorations. Higher up the road another arch bearing the mottoes " Success to the bride and bridegroom" and" Gad be with you both," and still higher up at the opening of the Walton Lea road the motto " Long life and much happiness" presen- ted itself on a very pretty arch. Another arch extended across the road at the principal lodge entrance. This arrangement, which reflected great credit on the workers, bore the mottoes " God bless the happy pair " and " Health and happiness." Inside the lodge gates, flags and flowers had been combined to figure out some vary pretty devices. From the porch door to the church an arch way had been put up and a large number of people, mostly ladies, .who are largely en evidence on these occasions, had assenablod and lined the passage to the church some considerable time before the ceremony, which took place at 215. The church rapidly began to fill, and long be- fore the arrival of the bridal party every seat in the sacred edifice was occupied. f While the guests were assembling Mr. Thomas Lane, the organist, played the following Programme: "Offertoire in E" (Batiste), oCatileres" (Jules Orison), " Military Polonaise" (Chopin), and the Bridal Chorus from "Lohengrin" (Wagner). At a quarter-past two the bridal carriage drove up to the entrance, and the bride was escorted into the church by her brother, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. She was attired in a handsome white satin dress, embroidered with silver and trimmed with Brussels lace. She wore a wreath of orange blossom and tulle veil, and carried a shower bouquet of white exotics, the gift of the bridegroom. Her ornament was a diamond crescent, also the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by two brides- maids, Miss P. E. Griffith(sister of the bridegroom) and Al iss Amy Whitley (cousin of the bride). They were dressed in pink and white striped silk skirts with chiffon bodices trimmed with !Abe rib- bon and cream coloured laze. Their hats were of cream Tuscan straw, trimmed with wreaths of for- get-me-nots and pink roses. They carried shower bouquets of roses, and wore gold bangles, with diamond and sapphire hearts, gifts of the bride- groom. The service was fully choral. The proces- sional hymn was" The voice that breathed o'er Eden" (to Kebel's music), and afterwards a psalm was sung to Dr.Hopkins' well-known chant. A new white altar frontal, the gift of the Vicar and Mrs. Darwall, was used for the first time on this occa- sion. The chancel and windows were very beauti- fully decorated with flowering plants, shrubs, and flowers. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. Thomas Whitly, who was assisted by the Rev. L. J T. Harwell, vicar of Walton. The bride was given away by her brother. The best man was Mr. Massey. At the conclusion of the service Mr. Lane played" Liebeslied " (Ilenselt) and Mendelssohn's Wedding March. After the wedding ceremony a reception was held at Walton Hall. The following is a list of the invited guests :—Mr. and Mrs. Cyril Greenali, Mr. and Mrs. Shiffner, Captain and Mrs. Griffith, Mrs. Tupper, Miss I Park, s'ies Griffith, Mrs. Park Yates, Mrs. and Miss Hall, the Rev A. Grier and the Misses Radcliffe, Mr. and Miss Tinsley, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. E. G. Davies, Rev. T. and Mrs. Whitley, Rev. H. T. and Mrs. Clarke, Mrs. W. C. Jones (the Rims), Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Jones and Miss Jones (the Oaklands), Mr. and Mrs. Hugh Jones, Mr, Owen Williams, ma% R. Wil- liams, Mr. and Aare. Peter Stubs, Mr. and Mrs. Mclver, Mr. I. Gree,nall, Master and Mies Greenall, Mr. Eltrereley, the Misses Greenall (Chester), Rev. Thchard an the Misses Greenall, Mrs. Harwell, and Master D. Darwall, Mr. and Mrs. Wynne Jones, Rev. H. V. and Mrs. Pigot, Master and the Misses Pigot, Mr. Charles white, Mr. Joseph Robinson, Mr. Rhodes, Mr. J. Whitley and Mr. H. Tinsley. . _

„ Later in the day the happy couple left for Loch Awe, Scotland, where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling dress was of biscuit•coloured crepon with a pale blue chiffon vest. She wore a hat trimmed with blue chiffon and black feathers. Appended is a list of presents :

div.head: EMBEZZLEMENT BY A WARRINGfON MAN.
div.p: EMBEZZLEMENT BY A WARRINGfON MAN.

At the Warrington Felice Court en Monday morning, before the Mayor (in the chair). Alderman Blackhuret I and Messrs. F. Monks, Birchall and Wright, Seth Garin- ston, vanman, 11, Dieort-street, was charged on a war- rant with having embnzled 103 and 143 ail from Messrs. Furness and Co., bakers and confectioners of Lythgoes-lane. Mr. F. R. Roberts appeared to prosecute, and defendant was represented by Mr. A. Browee, who reserved his plea. Mr. Roberts said the case was a very simple one. De- fendant was a vanman in the employ of prosecutors, and took out bread and collected money in the usual way. The customers had a book in which defendant had to enter the bread bought by them ram day to day. Ho also entered the amouet owing and gave receip:s for payment. Mr. Furness also had a book in which defendant entered the amounts he received from each customer. Ira that book there was the usual transfer sheet, which made a copy of the receipts. given to the customers, and that copy was handed to the employer with the money Defendant had entered the amounts he received in the cuetemers' book, but with regard to the receipt to be given to the employer he had made it out and the trans- fer had taken place, but instead of handing the first receipt to the customer he had destroyed it. 'fins cus- tomers were therefore not able to check the amounts entered. On the 13th June defendant received from a Mrs. Berridge, Padaate. the sum of £2 103. Defendant made out a receipt for £2. but instead of handing it to I the customer he destroyed it and handed to his employ( r the transfer. In the customers book appeared an entry of £2 103.,but the corresponding entry in the employers' book was only £2. Mrs. Berridge could not keep a cheek, simply because defendant had not given her a receipt Of course the fraud was sure to be found out in time. Defendant wen, on his holidays a week or so ago,and Aar. Furness's brother went round with the van and discovered what had been tale ne place. During the month of July, a Mrs. Joseph Batton paid lie. 6d , but that amount was not accounted for at all The only inference which could he drawn was that defendant had pocketed the money. On July 4th defendant received from Mrs. Hatton the sum of £1 7s. 10-led, and he only accounted for £1 5s Mrs. Berridge was being called, when Mr. Monks said there was a little irregu'arity. Defen- dant had neither pleaded guilty nor not guilty. Mr. Roberts thought that there should be a plea one way or the other. It would greatly simplify the case. Mr. Browne intimated that defendant pleaded not guilty. Harry Bolton Furness,a member of the firm of Messrs. Furness and Company, said defendant had b en in their employ since April 2nd. He received a weekly wage of 183., besides which he had a commission of 3 .1., in the £ on everything over £5. They received from derendaut £2, which he had entered as having received from Mrs. Berridge, and £1 53., instead of £1 7s. I.(q 1., from Mrs. Hatton. Mr. Browne.—l admit that. Witness added that the sum of us. 61, paid by Mrs. Hatton during the month of July was not accounted for. By Mr. Browne : Defendant had increased the besi- nese. Mr. Browne withdrew the plea of not guilty. He said defendant was 26 years of age, and had been brought up at a farm near Market Drayton with his father and mother. The father died some time ago, and the mother gave up the farm. One of her daughters was married and living in Warrington so he came to live here De- fendant first entered the employ of Mr. Boothroyd, and left him with the best of characters. During the time he had been with Messrs. Furness and Co he had in- creased the business,but had only received 18s pee we-.k and a commission, which latter was not worth troubling about. Defendant had not been betting,and he was not addicted to drink. His total defalcations did not amount to more than £2 or £3. Mr. Roberts said the amount was £7 or £B. Mr. Browse said defendant weut for his holidays earlier than he intended in consequence of his horse. be- ing ill,other wise he said he could have made up the de. ficiency. He did not offer that as an extenuating cir- cumstance, but he suggested that, as defendant had borne a geed character previously, he GhOU'd be dealt with under the First Offender's Act. He was the prin- cipal support of his mother, and he (Mr. Brewne)asked the magistrates to hi is lenient as pessible with him. Mr.Rob3rts said the prosecutors did not wish to prese the case unduly. They might have overlooked this offence, but money had been taken from them by other men, and they brought the case forward as a protest against the continual robbery to which they had been subjected. Mr. Monks wished to know why the firm had not had some better system for checaing the men. Mr. Rebuts said the firm thought the system was a perfect check. They could not improve upon it except by sending someone round. Mr. Browne said his client denied that the emlanzle- ment had been going on from the beginning of nis em- ployment. Mr. Monks (to Mr. H berts).—You say you have been subjected to this sort of thing before. I should have thought you would have given notice to your cus- tomers. Mr. Furies: explained that the previous thefts had taken place in the shop. Defendant was fined 40a. and costs, or in default of payment ordered to serve a mouth's imprisonment. Mr. Monks suggested that the firm shoeld send out weekly statements to their customers, with regard to any balance that might be owing. Mr. Browne mentioned that in a case in which he pro- secuted some little time ago, and in which the amount was £2O, a conviction was simply recorded. Mr. Birchall eaid this was a serious case. The Mayor thought defendant had been dealt with very leniently.

div.head: BAPTISMAL REGENERATION.
div.p: BAPTISMAL REGENERATION.

Sir,—ln your issue of the 23rd inst., there appears a letter over the non de guerre of " lona," on the above subject. I unt.esitatiogly attribute certain cffansive matter appearing m that letter,to the fact,that the writer appears to be soffering from an acute attack of the pre- vailing epidemic of 113rnan Fever. There is a statement, in the letter of " Ins," reearding the divine institution of the Sacrament of Baptism. which runs as fallows : " The ideztity of this teaching with that of the Church of England is so remarkable that we are compelled (Sic) to conclude that both churches founded it upon the same (Sic) traditions." Be leaves us in complete ignor- ance as to the nature of "the lame traditions." But I am sure, "boa" will be glad to hear, that the Catholic doc- trine of "Baptismal Regeneration," does not rest on traditions of any kind whatsoever. But is rather, laid down by Christ Himself in the inept unmistakable way possible. That baptism is of divine institution and fol- lows from the charge given by our Blessed Lord to His disciples! to baptize all nations in the name of the Father and the Son and of the Holy Ghost. (Matt. xxviii. 19.) Even before this injunction was given the disciples ad- ministered baptism (John iii 2, iv, 1,2); and they them- selves, doubtless, had received baptism before the Last Supper. The institution cf the sacrament may, in some way, be dated back to the baptism of our Lord in the Jordan, inasmuch as the matter was then defined and sanctified, and the form intimated 1)7 the manifesta- tion of the three divine persons, while the opening of heaven signified the supernatural effects of sacramental baptism. Baptism,on the authority of Christ,and of His apostles is called the sacrament of regeneration (John iii, 5). Furthermore, Christ our Lord says that a man must to born again of water and the Holy Ghost in order to b 3 saved (John iii, 5). Baptism is therefore necessary for salvation ; that is, as an ordinary means of salvation. A thing may be necessary for salvation either as a fulfilment of a divine precept (necessitas praTcepti), so that he who deliberately trangresses such precept by nis disobedience incurs the loss of his salva- tion; or it may be necessary as a means (necessitas medii), whereby the attainment of salvation is rendered possible. This means, again, may be absolutely or ordinarily necessary. It is absolutely necessary when it cannot be supplied by an other means; thus sanctifyirg, grace is necessary for salvation. When a means is required nnly in the ordinary course of divine providence, and may be exceptionally substituted by some other means, it is said to be necessary as an ordinary means. Such an exception, however, ob'ains only in the case in which the ordinary means ordained by God cannot be employed, and the express or implicit desire exists of employing the ordinary means if acces- sible. It is only as an ordinary means of salvation that baptism is necessary. Christ teaches without any res- triction thax "unless a man be born again of water and of the Holy Ghost he cannot enter into the King- dom of God." (John iii, 5 ) In this passage Chris* speaks of regeneration, or the origin of supernatural life, which is effected by baptism with water. Now supernatural life alone gives us the fitness for Salvation ; therefore baptism, which produces supernatural life, is necessary for salvation. This law is evidently universal. Christ speaks not, as in the Commandment to eat His flesh and drink His blood, of adults only. (John vi) Be simply asserts that baptism is necessary for all, consequently for infants, in order to obtain salvation (Mark it. 14.) Therefore, children who have not attained to the use of reason are to recover through the charity of others in the sacra- ment of baptism, that grace which they lost through the disobedience of another—their first father Adam.

That the Church of God has always held baptism to b 3 necessary for the salvation of all, even of infants, can easily be proved, but space will not permit me to do so on this occasion.—Yours truly, ----..-
SURSUI CORDA.

P.S. " Iona" seems to look upon all who teach the doctrine of "Baptismal Regeneration" as " Romanisers." Surely he is aware of the fact, that this doctrine is held by many low church people as well as Dissenters.
THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.

Sir,—ln support of the letter from Mr. E. L. Fleming which appeared in your last issue,permit me to say that, when I attended the first annual dinner of the secretaries of the Chambers of Commerce of the United Kingdom, held in London in March last, I was much impressed by the fact that practically every other chamber which was represented was numerically stronger than ourselves; and that, in spite of the legitimate boast that we are "the town of many industries" our list of members would not compare with those of places like Luton, Dudley, and Keighley. This is chiefly due to the cir- cumstance that, whilst in Warrington, our subscribers have hitherto been mainly manufacturers, in other towns all sections of the commercial community are included ; and several secretaries who were present informed me that they had as many as two or three hundred members. This, as they explained, enabled the Chambers which they represented, in addition to their ordinary functions, to provide a Public Reading Room, and to enlarge their sphere of usefulness in various other directions. In some, for example, a record of local stocks and shares and property sales was kept ; others had introduced a :labour bureau ; and nearly all were of opinion that periodical or permanent exhibitions of commercial samples might be started as an adjunct to the various Chambers. The local Chamber has for over twenty years been doing very useful werk in a quiet way, and has long ago se- cured the adhesion ef most of the principal manufac- turers of the district. If the list of members were suffi- ciently increased, and the Council more actively sup- ported by the general business community, there is not any reason whatever why Warrington should not enjoy the same advantages as other towns. I venture to think that there is no place in England which offers greater scope for an active and enlightened Chamber.—Faith- fully yours, ARTHUR BENNETT, Hon. Sec.

div.head: CYCLE ACCIDENT AT EAILLESTOWN.
div.p: CYCLE ACCIDENT AT EAILLESTOWN.

On Saturday evening Mrs. Davies, wife of Mr. George Davies, sawyer, of Earle-street, Zarlestown, was unfortunately knocked down by a bicycle and injured. She had been in poor health far some time and feeling slightly better, she went for a walk with her hasband. Darning out of the Mesnes and crossing the road under the Wargrave Bridge she saw a bicycle ridden by Mr. J. H. Profit corning down the hill at a good pace. She heard the warn- ing bell rung, but being seized with nervousness she could not get out of the way, and Mr. Profit being unable to avoid her, unfortunately knocked her down. She was very badly shaken, and one of her arms was much bruised at the elbow. She was carried into Mr. Holt' s cycle shop,and a cab having been procured she was conveyed home,and attended by Dr. Patterson, and is now recovering.

div.head: COLWYN BAY CONGO TRAINING INSTITUTR.
div.p: COLWYN BAY CONGO TRAINING INSTITUTR.

In connection with the above Institute the pur- pose of which is to give religious and industrial education in this country to the most promising of African Converts and to establish branch institu- tions on similar lines in Africa, Mission services were held in Earlestown on Saturday evening and Sunday. An open service was conducted on the Market place on Saturday night by the Rev. E. Jones Davies, who attended as a deputation from the Institute. He was accompanied by one of the African students, who also gave an address. They were present at che Baptist Church on Sunday morning, at the Co-operative Hall in the afternoon, when the African appeared in his native dress, and in the evening at the Christian Meeting room, and on the Market Place. Collections were made dur- ing the day in aid of the Institute, in connection with which an earnest appeal is wade for £5,000 in order to develop the work both at Colwyn Bay and in connection with the institutions already founded on the Dark Continent.

div.head: ST, HELENS.
div.p: ST, HELENS.
RESCUE BY Sr. HELENS POLICEMEN.

By the prompt action of a couple of- c--on.stables it is prob ibis that, in the earl 7 hours of Sunday morning at St. Helens, the lives of a man and his wife were saved. About a quarter to one o'clock ConstaVe Rigby, who was on duty in Liverpool-road, saw a large quantity of smoke issuing rum the bedroom of a lodging house,N). 15, Sandfield-crescent. Attacting the attention of Con- stable Sellars, both officers hastoned to the place and aroused the inmates. Rushing upstairs they found the bedclothes and bedsteads in one cf th° rooms on fire, a man and his wife in a half-stupefied condition occupy= leg the bed. These were got out in the nick of time and the fire extinguished with buckets of water. AFFRAY WITH NIGHT POACHERS.

At St. Helens County Police Cou-rt-Oti-S-a-tUrday,Henry Boardman and James Prior, colliers, of Billings, were charged with night poaching on land in the occupation of Mr. J. Appleton. at Crank,and Prior was also charged with assaulting John Yates, a gamekeeper. Mr. T. Garner (Messrs. Swift and Garner) appeared to prosecute on behalf of Colonel Richard Pilkington (mayor of St. Helens), who preserves the estate.—Mr. Garner stated thac between one and two o'clock that morning John Yates, gamekeeper, and three other men were watching on Appleton's land when till, saw six men co-ning along towards a Plantation. The gamekeepers went towards them, and bifore anything was said the men set upon them and the gamekeepers were violently assaulted. Is the struggle Prior struck Yates with a stick, and four of the men succeeded in escaping. A bag, containing live dead rabblts and some nets and sticks, wee mind. Evidence was given by Gamekeeper Yates and others. The prisoner Prior said that Yates set a doe o bim,and he was knocked to the ground. While he was on the ground Yates struck him on the head. The magistrates committed both men to .prison for :six weeks, and or. dered the nets to b 3 forfeited.
ATTACK ON A CONSTABLE,

At St, ftelens Police C mutt on 8 sturday, John Kerrigan and his wife Margaret, of Duke-court, Duke-stroet,were charged with assaulting Police-zonstable Mercer on Friday night.—The officer stated that about twenty minutes past eleven on the previous night he saw the prisoners creating a disturhanle in Duke-street. Kerri- gan, who was thrashing his wife, was spoken to by the officer, whereupon he seized him and in the struggle they fell to the ground together. The man kicked him severely about the legs and body, and Mrs. Kerrigan joined in the fray, holding the officer by the neck while her husband assaulted hitn. Richard Hall, a tram way inspector, went to the officer's assistance and blew his whistle, with the result that Constable Wilkes was at- tracted to the spot. Ho found Mercer thoroughly ex- hausted. The prisoners were taken to the police office, where Mercer fell down and was unconscious for two hours afterwards, lie had since been off duty. The two prisoners had been several times previously convic- ted, and the man was sent to prison for two months, and his wife for one month—both with hard labour. THE COLLIERY FATALITY AT.II.,YOnCS.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, on Saturday on the body of Thomas Caine, 31 years of age, collier, at Le.gh-street. Earlesto7n, who died from injuries re- ceived in the Wood Pit, Haydock, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. Evidence was given that on Friday afternoon Caine was engaged getting pi al n his working place, when a quantity fell upon him and he sustained injuries which resulted in his death some hours later. William Unsworth assistant fireman, said that Caine had not been ordered to get coals at the spot where he was injured, and he had no right to go there without instructions —George Rodgers, drawer, said he understood that Caine had instructions to widen hls working place,and he was doing that when the accident happened —Mr. Hall, the Government inspector, con- sidered that the accident was due to Caine's want of skill in coal-getting. He did not attribute it to want care so much as to want of skill.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

div.head: Tllt4 EXAMINER. FRIDAY, JULY 29, 198.
div.p: Tllt4 EXAMINER. FRIDAY, JULY 29, 198.
COMING OF AGE OF MISS GILLESPIE,
NEWTON.
INTERE3TING PR ESEN rA CION.

In connection with the attainment of the majority of Mica Clare Gillespie, only daughter of Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., Newton, an interesting presentation was made by the employe 3 of the paper works to that young lady, on Monday afternoon. The presentation was made in the works, and there were pr(sent--Mr. and Mrs. T. J. Gillespie, Captain 'Kenneth and Mrs, Gillespie Miss Clare Gillespie, Dr. Watkins, Mr. R. Barton, and employ6i. Mr. Barton. who initiated the proceedings, apologised for the absense of the Rev. H. Monk, who unfortunately had an engagement in Manchester. fie then proceeded to mention the different meetings that had taken place in that roorn,wh ch had mostly keen of a felicitous char- acter, amongst which was one 12 years ago, when he had a similar duty to that which had fallen upon hint that day. On the occasian to which he referred they presented their friend Cactain Gillespie with a token of their esteem upon his coming of age. He refer -ed to Mr. Gillespie's relationship with his workmen, and said that upon all occasions they bad been corseicuous for their , friendliness. Speaking of Mies Clare coming of age, he said it had been a privilege to many of them to see her growing up from childhood, and he thought he was j speaking the sentiments of the people of the Newton Paper Mill when he said they would watch with loving interest what the future might have in store for her. (Applause). Daniel Lairi,the oldest workman in the firm's employ in a very few words handed to Miss Gillespie,a handsome 'gold bracelet, and mentioned that the gift carried with it the feelings of every employ 6 at the wr,rks,and he ex- pressed the hope that she might bog live to enjoy the I use of the gift. Miss Gillespie said she could hardly find words to ex- press her thanks to them for Oil beautiful present they had made to her. She would always look upon it as bar most vilued possession seeing that it bore with it the kindly thoughts and good wishes of all the employ el of the Newton Paper Mill. Wherever she might be in the future she would always look upon it as a reminder of their gener )sity upon her 21st birthday. In conclusion she could only say that she hoped they would have the best ot weather on the trip she believed they were to have on the 20th August. (Cheers.) Mr. T. J. Gillespie said `ie was sure it would become a heirloom in his daughter's family and would be handed down from generation to generation. Whenever she wore it she would think of the kindness of those who gave her the present, and of the many happy years of life she had spent at Newton. He was glad to stand there amongst them, and to look back on the 313 years since his late partner and himself came there. Bo reflected that there had uot bran any occasion on which he recalled a single serious disagreement with the workers. They had worked pleasantly all along,and it was by no means the first occasion when a kindly meeting of that sort had been held,in fact as Mr. Barton had said, 12 years ago a similar pr. sent was given,when another member of his family had come of age. He re- ferred to the hearty co-operation of the workers when heavy demands had been made upon their time and capacity generally, and said that "all work and no play made Jack a dull boy." Mr. Barton and himself had been thinking of that old adage, and had decided they would give the employes a trip on the 20th August, at the cost of the firm, and he trusted they would be able to keep it regularly going and let it be a reminder of that occasion. (Cheers). Dr. Watkins referred to his long acquaintance with Mr. Gillespie which dated from Edinburgh where they played together on the old cricket ground. He was glad to be there that day knowing the family so intimately. The gathering then dispersed.

The usual weekly Session of the Temperance Mission Lodge, of the 1.0.G.T., was held on Wed- nesday in the Academy .street Mission-room. Bro. Roberts, C T., presided over a good attendance. Two candidates were initiated and one re-obligated. Bro. Tomlin read the D.C.T.'s quarterly circular, which was accepted. Bro. J. Sheath reported having visited the "Great Heart " Lodge, St Helens, and presented the fraternal greetings of that lodge which were accepted. PRESENTATION TO MR. T. W. Cits.tvrnr. There was an interesting gat).ering on Tuesday in Sr. Paul's Infant School, Rolleston-ttreet, when Mr. T, W. Chantry (son of Mr. William Chan'xy, baker, confectioner, &c., Sankey-street and Hors - market-street), was the recipient of a handsome present on the occasion of his recent marriage with Miss E. A. Clayton, of Liverpool. The present took the form of a very handsome marble timepiece,with bronze ornaments to match (supplied through Mr. Alfred Woods), and which bore the following in- scription :—" Presented to Mr. Thomas W. Chantry by the employes of Messrs. Chantry and Son, War- rington,on the occasion of his marriage, July 14th, 1898." About 45 of the employes of the firm at- tended the proceedings, which took the form of a conversazione, amongst those present in addition to the employe, being Mr. and Mrs. W. Chantry, Mr. and Mrs. Clayton, the Rev. H. V. and Mrs.Pigot,Mrs. Briefly, the Misses Chantry, Ashurst, and Westwell, Mr Ernest Wilkes (organist) and Mrs. Wilkes, and Mr. W. and Miss Brough. Speeches were delivered, after which excellent refreshments were partaken of, followed by singing and dancing, and the pro- ceedings were of a most interesting and enjoyable character.

On Monday evening a very enjoyable converse- zione in connection with the above church was held in the day schools, Old-road,when there was a large attendance of members of the congregation and others. The proceedings commenced at eight o'clock by an exhibition of snap-shots taken by the Vicar (the Rev. F. Slater) during the summer, and shown with the lantern on hie new daylight screen. Miss 1 Eate Beesley followed with a recitation, entitled " Hanging a Picture," and during the evening she I gave with much (If 'ct " The Story ef a Stowaway," and "The Widow Cummiskey." Miss B. Eckersley, a daughter of a member of the congregation, made her second appearance in public, and she acquitted herself re- markably well. The accompanists were Mrs. Atkin, Miss Slater, and Miss Reynolds. his 005 NNW RAPID CYCLES.—Gialawn, 51, Bridge-street. Warrington. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A. CHILD AT WARRINGTON. On Thursday morning at the Police Parade Room, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the death of Ethel Senior, 3 years, who met with an accident on Tuesday whieh ended fatally.—John Henry Senior, blacksmith, 1, Scott-street, Warring- ton, father of the deceased, said he last saw his child alive on Tuesday afternoon about ten minutes Past one. Be next saw her in the Infirmary dead. She had bean in company with her sister Mary Jane (11 years.)—George Mortimer, 2-4, Rodney-street, Warrington, said he saw the accident on Tuesd. ay afternoon in Lythgoe's-lane. The child was coming up Haydoek-street and came from behind a float which was standing at Furness and CYS. shop, and before the driver of the dray and two horses could pull up, she had got under the horse's feet and was knocked down.—Mary Jane Senior, sister of the deceased, eaid she was with her sister Ethel and Florence Littlewood. They crossed the street, where a van was standing opposite Farness's shop. Ethel left go of her hand and they were nearly on the parapet when the horse caught her. They did not see the horses coming.—John Dolbean, 9, Derby Cottages, Holt, Rainhill, said he was driving two horses and a waggon for Messrs. Matthew Hayes and Conning. Limited, herb beer manufacturers. He was coming along Lythgoes-lane. He was driv- ing about six or seven miles an hour, slightly up- hill, and when passing the float just as the horse's heads reached half-way along the float the child came from behind. Lie did hie best to pull up, hut the near horse struck the child who was krocked between the two and carried some distance, and the off-side wheel ran over it.—Annie Ellis, nurse. said the child was brought into the Infirmary about twenty minutes to five o'clock. She died shortly after admission.—After consideration the jury brought in a verdict of" Accidental death." and added that no blame was attached to the driver.
