Mr. Ormend stated that FL Eddington, who had gained 9 marks during the Session under notice. had obtained a similar number in a previous Session, when he_carried off the gold medal.

Mr. Stott, in proposing a vote of thanks to the donors to the ptiza fund, said he had had great experience of prize distributions, having been engaged in the work of Science teaching for over 20 years, and the prizes which had been distributed that night were the finest lot of prizes he had Seen distributed to so few people, and the donors to the fund deserved their thanks, as they had ' done well, and it only remained for the students to deserve the prizes. At Legh the prize list was £24 to be divided amongst 900 people, whilst at Earlestown they had £45 to be divided among 300 people, and this fact would help them to gauge the generosity of the donors. The Earle-town students were as good as they were any- where else, an perhaps a little better, and the one thing they had to contend with in their evening Science Classes was the want of preliminary education before the subjects were undertaken. That handicapped the teachers very much in their work. The elementary education given in the day schools was a failure as re- garded the classes, he did not moan to say that it was a failure in itself, as the amount of good it did was incal- culable, but the subjects taught in the day schools did not go far enough. Take for instance the one subject of arithmetic. This one subject required to be pushed much further, as boys and girls came out of school knowing almcst nothing about monsuration. What were they to do if a student did not understand how to got the circumference of a wheel from its diameter. If they had good secondary education in the town it would remedy this. In the evening (lasses they had a class in mathematics, which was a subject which ought to he taken up by every student who wanted to attain to any perfection in Building Con- struction and machine drawing. Any student who passed the elementary in building construction and machine drawing could understand a working drawing, but if he wanted to become a foreman or roaster he must go much further and study mathematics. The Science and Art Department had introduced another subject in this branch which they called Elomentary Practical Mathematics, but they had made a mistake in not beginning at the beginning and 5. student ceuld not tactile that subject until he had passed the first stage,when he would find it very interesting. He doubted whether the people of the district appreciated the classes as they ought. They were not simply classes for boys, there were hundreds of workmen in the works who might benefit from the classes, He knew there was a lot of hard work about them and everybody could not rise to he foreman or master by reason of the work he did at the classes, but he would make a very much better workman, and take more pleasure in his work after at- tending the class. (Applause.) Mr. Smalley seconded, and the vote was unanimously passed.

Mr. W. Thompron jun., moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Collingwood. who he said was the head of a large engineering works in the district, and had had a very large experience abroad in such work, and he knew as well as anybody the advantage of technical education in this country. Dr. Patterson seconded and the vote was heartily accorded.

Mr. 6-311(ng-w—o-od acknowledged the vote, and pro- posed the similar compliment to the Chairman which was carried nem. con. The students afterwards held a ronVersazione, at which light refreshments were handed ound.

They wore honoured by a visit from the Grand Treasurer, Mr. G. Higham, the organiiing agent, Bro D. Houghton, and a large number of influential brethren from Warrington and reaketh Lodges. N. G. A. Rough. sedge presided, and n number of candidates submitted themselves as members, and were initiated by the Grand Treasurer.
After the ordinary lodge buoinese had been disposed of the meeling Wa9 thrown open t) the public, and very soon tho torn WA* crowded.

The Cnairm an intro luced the Grand Treasurer,espres• sing his pleasure at meeting so Listinguished an officer of the Order, and said he reeardeol it as a good omen for the success of the new lodge. The Grand Treasurer was received with applause. He said he thought he could not do better than address a few words of adviee to the young members present. When young in offi.le, soiree 39 years ago, some one told him he was too young to have anopinion. He replied that time would soon remedy that fault, and now as he was growing grey ia the service of Druidism, he email strive to advise and -.lounsel others. was pleased to be present at this meeting., the formation of the Lodge being attributable to the ap- pointment of Brother D. Boughton as organizing agent. This was a pet scheme of his as he considered it the best means of bringing the benefits of the order to districts that were greatly lacking in this respect. He should be most willing to give Brother Houghton what help he could and would visit willingly where convenient. (Ap- plause.) He asked the members to do all they could for the 'Lodge. They should elect the best men for the offices amd should -look well alter the sick and manage- ment Ronde and try to bs as careful as possible in the latter. E‘ch brother should see that he got all the ad- vantages promised to him, The advantages wFrs numer- ous,sick pay, travelling expectses,and to brothers, unfor tueately out of work,assistance was never refused and in many cases new work had been found for them. (Linoleum) As Druids thee should work together,advis- ! ing and helping were ne•dful as they had been counselled in the initiatory ceremony. He hoped that the new lodge would eventually equal the mother lodge. Nothing was more conducive to success than the individual effort of I the members. Every brother should feel, when intro- ducing a new taadidate that he was not only doing good for his Lo lee, but bestowing an ine a'culable benefit on that candidate. He wished the Lodge and the brothers armed him every success. (Loud Applause.) 13'011'r Appleton moved a vote of thanks to the Grand Treasurrr for his able address and assured the members that althoee.h he had been a member of the Lolge fo- over 0 years and taken part in many gather- ings connec'ed with the Order, nerhing gave him more pleasure than to assist in every way the formation of a new Lodge and to assure a Druidical welcome to the rand Officer. Bro. Coo way seconded the resolution. _ . . .

--- The Organizing Agent, Bro. D. Houghton, supported it by request of the new members who desired to be associated with the sentiments expressed, regarding the honour they felt at the visit of Bro. Higham to their lodge and the pleasure and interest they had all felt in listening to his address on the duties of all members to the lodge and the welfare of the society. He personally thanked the G. T. for his presence as he regarded it as compliment to him, that he should have presided at the first lodge inaugurated since big appointment as Or- ganizing Agent. . _

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. [BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT ] CRICKET.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. [BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT ] CRICKET.

Newton made a week-day fixture last week with Leigh,and in order to secure victory, engaged the services of one or two county players who were dis- engaged for the day. It is only to be expected, under the circumetances, that Leigh would not pre- vail against such an arrangement of talent,but they made on excellent stand, and were able to secure a draw,

Theirrival, Earlestown,w—ho by the way,they en- eoßnter next week, wore badly beaten by Liverpool on Saturday. From some cause or other the Earles- town season has been a disastrous one, as out of all the matches which have been played so far they have only been able to score a couple of wins. Liver- pool had the advantage of a clean wicket and as the bowling of the Earlestown men was at no time of a dangerous nature they managed to pile on 133 before they were dismissed. Earlestown could only total up 61, and out of these Crowther made 21, his innings being marked specially for patience and clever hitting,

On Monday Earlestown journeyed to Old Trafford to'try conclusions with Manchester club. The ordin- ary playing team was strengthened by the addition of oEllar and Bate, but in batting they proved of no assistance as they were both easily disposed of for ducks. Earlesto wn managedYto get together a score of 116, towards which Jenkinson contributed 30, his hits being remarkable for their lustiness. Manchester put on a strong eleven and when they went to the wicket, they soon began to institute the healthy pastime of leather hunting,and for the loss of six wickets scored 452. Mitchell the wicket- keep, surprised his colleagues, for dispensing with the pads, he took the ball and captured 3 wickets.

The second team are doing much better than the first, and after disposing ot Garswood for 92, they went in and totalled 60 for the loss of 2 wick etQ, and, had time allowed, would certainly have piled on a big score.

The Primitive Methodists eleven will certainly have tsl hunt round the haunts where cricketers do dwell, is they wish to figure in the annals of cricket as wielders of the supple willow. So far they have not done well,and there is a grand oppor- tunity for improvement.
Their confreres, the Wesleyan club, do rather better, and on Saturday they managed a draw in their favour with the Sankey Bridges Wesleyans.
CYCLING.

The social combination from amongst the Wes- leyan body for the purpose of instituting the social cycling trips. bad a most enjoyable run last week to Frodsham. They include ladies, and as speed is only a minor factor, they are in no hurry to reach the end of their journey. On the run in question, they took 2- hours to go 15 miles, but they had so much extra enjoyment, and home was reached a little after 10/o'clock.
This was a much better run than the previous one wnen they got astray on the road to Lvmm, about which perhaps it would be best to say little.

The Cycle Parade Committee are hard at work, and all the preliminaries are advanced. It only ueeds a line day, and a large and generous crowd to make the affair a 81.1CCGO98. The committee are hop- ing that all cyclists within a radius of 20 miles will come and help them on August 27th, aad thus help the old folks to a good treat.

div.head: CLERGY DAUG-HFE gS' SCHOOL.
div.p: CLERGY DAUG-HFE gS' SCHOOL.
REUNION, 1898.

Od Monday a re•union in connection with the above school was held, and proved to be very enjoyable. At twelve noon a service attended by the present and a number of former pupils was held in the College chapel, conducted by the Rector the Rev. Canon Willis),assisted by the Rev, A. A. Markham, who read the lesson. The lesser Litany was gone through, and the pupils gave an excellent rendering of the anthem "Lift thine eyes." The hymns sung were 270 (processional), 437, 367, and 379 (recessional). The address was delivered by the Rev. J. J. Langham, who chose for his text the words " For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not yet seen are eternal.' The, service over, tho afternoon and evening were spent in a very agreeable manner, in the College and grounds.
MEETING OF SUBSCRIBERS AND PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

The anniversary of the institutions of the Warrington Clergy Widows and Orphans. and Clergy Daughters' School, was held on V‘,ednesday, nreiide I over by Mr. R. Jovnsin. There were also present :—Canon Penrhyn, The Lord Bishop of Chester, Canon Willis, Archdeacon VVoosnam, Rev. R. Greenall, iv, Carson, Mr. if. Gre (treasurer), Mr. John White. Mr. James Tinsley, Mr. W. P. Fullagar, Rev. E C. E. Carleton, Canon E R. Betlitel Jones, Mr. John Kendall, Mr. J. Alderson Smith, Canon Blundel and. Canon Spooner. ' '
The days proceedinas commenced with a meeting of subscribers at 11 o'clock.
CLERGY WIDOWS AND ORPHANS' FUND.

The Rev. Canon PEINRHYN (hon secretary of the Clergy Widows and Orphans' Pen-ion Fund) reported : —Since our last anniversary two of our oldest and most constant members of the committee have been called to their rest—Archdescon Anson and Canon Birley. We desire now to place on record our sense of the value of their services, and of the loss we have sustained in their removal. We would sugyst that they should be suc- ceeded by the Rev A. G. Rawthorne, rector of Croston, and the Rev. E. Eloskyns, of Bolton. No other names having been submitted to the Secretaries, thu retir- ing members are re-elected, as under, subj Pet to the confirmation of this annual meeting :—Cbester : Rev It Greenall, Rev Canon B!encowe, Messrs. James Tinsley and J. H. Crofton ; Manchester : Rev. Hon, A. Lyttrlton, Rev. E. floskyos V. Birley and Messrs. H. W. Worley Taylor and W. P. Fullagar.Liver- pool, Rev. Canon Armour, Rev. Canon Blundell,' he Earl of Lathom. and Mr. R. Ireland Blackburne. OF those who were aided last year, one (a Chester orPhem) has been married : tw ) (Manchester orphans) have died;two (Chester widows) have sent in no application ; and four in acccriance with notice last year, have had their ' grants disallewed. There ore two new widows' applications from Manchester, one from Chester and three from Liverpool, as well as one orphan. The annual meeting is asked to sanction pensions, donations, and payments for free scholars at the Clergy Daughters' School to the amount of £2.090 (exactly the same as last j year), and if the recommendations of the committee are approYed,there will be on our list from ChesterlB widows I and 12 orphans from Manchester 30 widows and 20 orphans,from Liverpool 14 widows and nine orphans, and free education for six orphans—two from Chester, two from Manchester, and two from Liverpoel. The income for the year ended December 31st, 1897, was £2,025 23. 6d. Tnis total shows again a further falling off of income of about £lOO from the previous year, and the diminution affects all the three chief POLITO'S, church collections, donations, and subsciiptions. We would, therefore, earnestly appeal to all our friends,lay as well as clerical, to procure us increased support and new subscribers,es otherwise we chat! compslled, however unwillingly,to cut down grants which we hitherto have made,and which in many cases we feel ought rather t.) be increased.

The PRESIDENT, in moving the adoption of Canon Pen. rhyrfs report, said it was with deep regret that they heard of the falling off of the income of about £llO He felt very keenly about the matter, and hoped they would not allow the falling off to continue. (Hear, hear). Mr. FULLAGAR seconded, and said he also regretted the falling off in the subacriptiona and the general support to institutions. He spoke especially for the Manchester diocese, with which he was connected. He was sorry to say that the rece;pts from the Manchester diocese were not what they ought to be. They received in Manchester a great deal more than the other dioceses, and yet they did not do as much. He had tried to show that the institutions should get their share from the diocesan Sunday, hut he was very sorry to say that the Bishop of Manchester had not at present seen his way to sanction such an idea. People got it into their heads that the institutiona were for the benefit of the people of Warrington only, and did not remember the valuable werk they were doing for the three dioceses. He supported the appointment of corn- mittees, especially ladies' committees, tr. take the matter up for the purpose of raising funds. (Hear, hear). The upon was then adopted:
REPORT OF THE COAIMITTEE OF MANAGEMENT.

The Rev. Canon Intim, hon. secretary of the Clergy Daughters' School, presented the following report of the Committee of Management of that institution :—The ex- cellent report of the examination of the school by the Oxford delegates for 1897, though read at the annivers- ary last year, arrived too late for any comment upon it in your commiitee's report to the subscribers, as did the results of the Cambridge and Oxford Local Examine.tions. This was unfortunate, as it prevented that lic expression of satisfaction which was due to the mime]. and so well deserved by the head mistress and her staff for the very high praise that was therein given. This year vour comnsittee are more fortunate. The results of the drawing and music examinations, held in June and Jely,ere to hand, and considering the respec- tive ages of the pupils will be found to compare favour- ably with those of last year. The report of the examina- tion of the school held last week by the Oxford Delegacy has also ceme,and is again excellent, hut as the results of the Oxford and Cambridge Locals will not be forth- coming until August it is impossible to give that full and complete account of the school's condition and successes which on an occasion like this is so much to be desired. The health of the school is very Batisfactory,the conduct all that could be desired, while the numbers, which rose last year from 34 to 47, are now 39, and will be proba- bly 45 at the beginning of next term. The services have been held as usual in the Parish Church and school chapel during the past year, and the Bible classes con- ducted whenever practicable. Five candidates were con- firmed by the Bishop of the diocese in the spring. The annual remeirm service was held on Monday, July 25th, when about 50 former students, in addition to present members were in attendance.

Tue PRESIDENT moved the adoption of this report,and said they must all feel gratified to know that the school was increasing in numbers. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON (Warrington) seconded, and said the successes which hail been obtained were only to be expected under the present management. The school was regarded as one of the best in the north of England.
VOTE OF THANES TO THE PRESIDENT. A SUGGESTION TO INCREASE THE FUNDS.

Mr. HENRYGREENALL, in proposing a vote of thanks to the President for the excellent manner in which he had conducted the business cf the meeting, said Mr. Fullagar had referred to his despondency. He thought there was same reason in it. There was about £9O increase against the treasurer for the past year, and an adverse balance due to the treasurer on the Clergy Daughters' School of £825, en that they were going to the bad at the rate of about £2BO a year. Mr. Greenall concluded by announcing the handsome donati )n 430: £5O from the President towards the funds—£2s for the Clergy Daugh- ters' School and £25 for the Widow and Orphans' Fund. , (Arplause), , Mr. Join; WHITE seconded the motion, and said they I were all indebted to the President for his liberal contri- bution. They took up the question of the deficiency at each annual meeting, and the same words were said —almost word for word—hut he thought they ought to take some steps to bring the institutions more before the dioceses. The suggestion Mr. Fullagar had made about the appointment of committees was a very good one. It had been suggested that there should be an organizing secretary appointed to go about to advo- cate the claims of the inatitutions,but sometimes organ- izing secretaries were expensive luxuries. However, in the present case he thought it would be advisable to have one fora year or two.

-• The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said he had come to the conclusion that the weakest point in the institution was the manner in which the members were elected on the committee ;it had become a kind of nomination. No doubt they got excellent men, hut it was not the way in which they could get interest aroused in the institutions or bring home to the Churchmen generally their respon- sibility. A plan should be devised whereby the various deaneries in their conferences could be compelled to elect =embers on the committee, and that would necessitate their claims being brought before the meetings from time to. time. There was something radically wrong with the clergy themselves in not taking sufficient in- terest in the charities.

The Rev.;. CARSON suggested that the clergy th.m. selves, each In his own ncihbourhood, sholld call upon the laity awl ask for subscriptions from these who did not already subscri"o. (Hear, hear). Mr. FULLAGAR promised to do what he could to uree the claims of the institution, and after some further dis- cussion the vote of thanks to the President was put and heartily agreed to, and the meetinz of subscribers ter- minated.
!SERVICE IN THE PARISH CHURCH. Divine service was afterwards held in the Parish Church, when the Rev. Canon H. Blackburne (vicar of Crewe Green) preached an able sermon.

THE DINNER. Dinner was afterwards provided in the Clergy Daugh- ters' School, the arrangemrnte For Which were entirely satisfactory, the whole pass.ing off in a very agreeable manner. Mr. D. Morrie. Wilderspool-road, supplied the waiters.
